s01.slug: MONDAY · 9:10 AM · LAS OLAS FIRE STATION, TRIGO ROAD — THE SANDBAG PILE
body: A shower crosses the firehouse lot, and goes, and comes back, and in the gaps the asphalt steams. Behind the Las Olas station on Trigo Road the county has dumped a hill of sand the size of a bungalow and thrown a blue tarp over it, held down at the corners with truck tires, and a bedsheet on two sawhorses says in marker what the hill is for: FREE SANDBAGS · 10 PER HOUSEHOLD · BRING YOUR OWN SHOVEL. The line of pickups at the curb runs back past the Chevron. It is nine in the morning on Martin Luther King Day, and half of Las Olas has come out in its rain boots to be told to take ten.

On top of the hill, in a Ziploc with the zipper pinched around its cord, Theo’s iPhone is playing something quick and bright out of its one small speaker to a lot full of shovels. He set it there himself at half past eight and told it to stay.

Sigma Rho has come in force. At the foot of the hill the pledges fill burlap in two lines, in ponchos with SIGMA RHO ironed across the back in gold over their navy blazers, and up and down the lines walks Brooks Callahan, the senior, in a visor in the rain, with a clipboard sealed in a dry-cleaner’s bag and a laminated sheet he holds up whenever a shoulder droops. SERVICE IS A FORM OF BROTHERHOOD, the sheet says, in a typeface that has been to a good school.

Theo is at the end of the second line, shoveling with his right hand. In his left, held level against his chest, is a white china teacup with a raw egg in it, HOLLIS lettered down the shell in blue ballpoint. The rules, as Theo has recited them twice since seven, are that Hollis never leaves his person outdoors, so Hollis has come to the sandbags, and Theo has been shoveling one-handed for an hour with the easy economy of a boy who has decided to be good at it and make it look like nothing.

Jack is two bags from the end of the line in the Carhartt, gone dark across both shoulders, with a borrowed shovel and mud to the knees that will be going to Mass at noon. At seven Theo had stood over his bed in the poncho, cup in hand, and explained that a pledge earns a point for every civilian he brings, and that Jack was the only civilian he knew who could be trusted with a shovel the right way up. Jack had his jeans on before the explanation was over.

Kevin is here because Jack texted him at ten past seven. He has come in a rain shell zipped to the chin with a Costco bag of work gloves, six pairs, the sizes in Sharpie on the cuffs, and he has been going down the lines pressing them on people. “Burlap and wet hands is how you get contact dermatitis,” he tells a pledge who has declined. The pledge takes the gloves. On the first line Margot, in a black slicker with the hood up and her Docs sunk to the ankle in wet sand, is filling bags at a rate the pledges gave up trying to match around eight-thirty. She came on her own. She has told everyone who asked that she is observing service as performance, and she has filled more bags than anyone on the lot without once looking up to observe anything.
A firefighter comes down the line in a yellow slicker, young and solemn, and stops in front of the teacup. He studies it. “Captain wants to know,” he says, “if the egg needs a bag.”
“Please tell the Captain that Hollis is in the care of a fraternity,” Theo says.
“Is that better?”
“It’s the same as being in the care of no one,” says Theo, “with nicer stationery.”
The firefighter writes nothing down. From the hose bay, a minute later, comes the sound of several men not laughing.

Brooks has gone down on one knee in the wet with a digital camera to get the ponchos against the sky for the chapter website. “Look like you mean it, gentlemen!” he calls. “Brotherhood!” The shutter clicks, and a pledge in mid-shovel has to go and find his face.
“Service,” Theo says, to the sand, “is just Brooks’s word for *seen*. All charity is a tax on looking good, Costigan. This one has a camera.”

Margot doesn’t look up. “In 1968 a man preached an entire sermon on exactly that, Vance,” she says. “The wish to be out in front and be seen. His argument was that you don’t kill it. You choose what you’re seen doing.” A bag lands on the stack. “He said, ‘Everybody can be great, because anybody can serve.’” She is already reaching for the next one.
Theo shovels through a bag or two of that. “Then I’d like it known,” he says, “that I am very great, and I am holding an egg.”

“Sandbagging,” Kevin says, to the lot at large, working a glove onto the nearest pledge, “which is what Theo does at cards, but for the community.” The lot does not laugh. A squall goes across it. “The tarp was dripping on my timing,” Kevin says.

The RAZR went off twice against Jack’s thigh at nine minutes to nine, and he has felt the place ever since, through the denim and the weather. Now he steps in under the lip of the tarp, where the sand is dry, and pulls one glove off by the fingers and thumbs the phone open.

body: He stands under the dripping tarp a minute longer than the text needs, and then he puts the phone away and the glove back on and picks up the shovel.

Down the line there is a long dry tearing sound, and Theo’s bag lets go along the seam. Sand pours out over his shoes in a hiss. He looks at the burlap, and then at the shovel in one hand and the teacup in the other, and does the arithmetic. “Costigan,” he says, reasonably. “I find myself a hand short of a civilization.”

choices.text: “Give him here.”
response: Jack peels off the other glove and takes the cup in both hands. It is warm from Theo’s palm, a thing he would not have guessed, and the egg shifts once and settles with HOLLIS facing him. “Level,” Theo says. “Level, Costigan.” Then Theo has two hands and a shovel, and the burst bag is a heap and the next one is a bag, and the line fills on around them for twenty minutes by the firehouse clock, with the rain coming and going on the rim of the cup and Jack’s elbows locked at his ribs.
Theo doesn’t look up from the work. “If he hatches in your care,” he says, “he’s yours.”
Margot goes by with a bag under each arm and glances at the side of Jack’s head without breaking stride. “You have sand in your ear, Costigan. Both of them.”

choices.text: “Does Hollis know it’s a federal holiday?”
response: “He’s been briefed,” Theo says. “His position is that a holiday with a shovel in it is a Tuesday in a hat.” He kneels, pins the split bag against his thigh with the cup tucked in the crook of his arm, gathers the burlap shut with his shovel hand and ties it off in a knot he must have been taught by someone who disliked him. Brooks, passing behind the clipboard, makes a small mark and moves on.

Margot has stopped beside Jack with a full bag on her shoulder. “A federal holiday,” she says, “is the one day a year we agree to be good to each other on purpose. You have sand in your ear, Costigan. Both of them.”

choices.text: *Take the shovel. Fill his bags for him.*
response: He takes the shovel out of Theo’s hand without a word. Theo opens his mouth and shuts it and takes the cup in both hands, and for the next stretch Jack fills bags for two, his own and then Theo’s, in long scoops, the hill coming down a shovelful at a time. “Civilians don’t count toward your bags, Vance,” says Brooks, behind the clipboard, making a mark. Theo does not care, and says so with his face.
Margot sets a finished bag on the stack beside Jack’s and looks at the stack, and then at him. “You have sand in your ear, Costigan. Both of them.”

s02.slug: MONDAY · 12:10 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — THE 12:10
body: A squall gets to the roof a minute before he gets to the door. St. Brendan’s is nearly all roof, an A-frame pitched so steep the shingles come most of the way to the ground, and inside, the sound comes down both slopes and meets over the nave, like the underside of the bleachers at Mooney on a wet Friday in October. He’s late. One of the Knights is at the ambo with the first reading, leaning down into the microphone to be heard over it until it passes: Samuel, taking the kingdom away from Saul. *Obedience is better than sacrifice.*

Coming across the courtyard he passed Newman’s table under the overhang: the Haiti baskets again, a stack of flyers going soft in the wet, a poster board with the text-to-give number on it in Kenzie Rourke’s bubble letters, and Kenzie behind it in a clear poncho, who waved with her entire arm. He isn’t working the table today, but he stopped long enough to put the five from his wallet in the jar and let Kenzie tell him the running total, to the cent, through the poncho; Newman is his too, and he’s not giving it up to anybody. His jeans are stiff to the knee with sand from the pile on Trigo Road, and he came in by the side door with the hood of the Carhartt still up.

It’s a holiday and a weekday, and the 12:10 on a day off is the regulars and the weather: the three widows who say a rosary in the front pew before every Mass, two Knights in their windbreakers, a mother walking a baby up and down the side aisle, half a dozen students in wet sweatshirts, Becca Lindell among them in a COEUR D’ALENE hoodie across the aisle. Lena is two-thirds of the way up on the Lady’s side, by herself, the Haiti clipboard on the kneeler beside her and her hair dark at the ends from the courtyard. Julian doesn’t come to weekdays.
He is done with Lena Broussard. He decided it on Saturday.
He takes the last pew.

Osei reads the Gospel himself, in the green. People want to know why John’s disciples fast and his don’t, and Jesus talks about a wedding, and a bridegroom, and then about cloth, and then about wine. *Likewise, no one pours new wine into old wineskins. Otherwise, the wine will burst the skins, and both the wine and the skins are ruined. Rather, new wine is poured into fresh wineskins.*

On a weekday he preaches from where he stands, one hand on the ambo, and gives them three sentences. “Today the country keeps the birthday of a preacher who told it the check had come back marked *insufficient funds*, and all week we have watched Port-au-Prince sleep in the street, and I do not believe the Lord keeps those two in separate books. The new wine is what God does to old skins. It splits them — ask anyone he has ever been poured into — and it is still wine.”

One of the widows reads the intentions off an index card in a voice that has read them for forty years: for the people of Haiti, the dead and the ones still under the concrete and the ones digging with their hands; for the dream of Dr. King, that it be fulfilled; for the sick of the parish, by name, a long list of first names. *Lord, hear our prayer.* Under the patter on the roof it comes back from a couple of dozen people, ragged, and Jack’s voice in it, from the back.
*I want to want to*, he told this man through a linen screen on Saturday. The wine in the Gospel doesn’t ask the skins what they want.

At the sign of peace the mother with the baby turns around in the pew ahead and gives him her free hand, and the baby, asleep in the sling, gives him nothing. Across the aisle Becca leans out over the end of her pew with her hand out, as she always does, and he takes it. Two-thirds of the way up Lena turns to shake the hand behind her, and there’s no one behind her for three rows, and she turns back to the front and folds her hands on the clipboard.

At Communion he stays on his knees while the few pews in front of him empty, and says Nonna’s prayer for the ones who can’t go up, the whole of it, under the hymn the widows carry without the organ. Lena, coming back along the side aisle toward her pew, is facing the back of the church, and he’s in front of her, on his knees, the only one left in his row. She looks at the floor ahead of her the rest of the way.

It comes as she turns in to her pew. Not the song — he keeps the song where he keeps it — but her eyes in December, across the Bastille, through the second chorus, dry, and his own meeting them and holding, through to the last chord.
Friday he was at the Rialto with Skye, and the Bastille was somebody else’s night. It doesn’t seem to matter.

He leaves at the blessing, while Osei’s hand is still in the air over the widows, by the side door. Across the courtyard the Newman table sits under its overhang with a dish towel over the baskets, and behind it Kenzie, hood up, is reading one of her own flyers. The shower has gone over. The overhang drips along its edge, one bead at a time, and the wet flagstones from the side door to the table shine.

s03.slug: MONDAY · 7:50 PM · DELGADO HALL, 420 — THE HUB BEFORE THE HUB
body: The clock goes first: four beeps and a pulse, tinny, out of the one working speaker of a thirteen-inch Sanyo on Doug Pruitt’s dresser, and all of 420 leans toward it like a congregation at the elevation.

Twenty minutes earlier, Jack comes up through the lobby with his hood up and doesn’t slow down at the glass of the Fishbowl, where ABC is cued up for *The Bachelor*: Laney on the middle couch with the remote aimed at the set like a sidearm, and Lena on the arm beside her with her feet drawn up on the cushion. Both faces stay on the screen. He takes the stairs.
There are two people in this building he goes around now, since Saturday, and both of them are on that couch. Everybody else he goes looking for, and tonight everybody else is upstairs.

On the east stairs, between three and four, the RAZR starts going in his hand, one text on top of the next. The clock on the little screen says twenty to eight, twenty to eleven in Youngstown, a holiday night, when Gina stops pretending to sleep.

body: He hasn’t seen the pictures. He knows what’s in them anyway, because she told him the plan on Ocean Road on Sunday: a table, a man from the network, a dress that came by messenger, and a girl alone in all of it, because that was the deal. He can see his mother at the kitchen table in the blue light of the Dell with a dish towel over her shoulder and her mouth a straight line; that is as far as she will go in front of Gina. Nonna’s Italian he can supply himself; he heard it once about Gina’s homecoming dress.

The fourth text is the one he stands still for. By the fifth his thumb has found the bump on the bridge of his nose: Tommy Hritz, St. Christine’s, who broke it in the eighth-grade CYO game, has shared his girlfriend. He shuts the phone on all of it and doesn’t answer a one.
On four the lounge is no good: the television is dark, with Priya’s newest laminate taped across the glass of it, CABLE OUT. DO NOT “FIX.” He knocks on 420.
“Doug. You have a TV.”

The door opens on a dark room and a cloud of onion. “Duuude,” Doug says, over about five vowels. “You’re *also* Jack.” He holds the door wide with a Funyun, as though the universe has finally sent him the other half of the pun.

Kevin is cross-legged on his own bed with *Organic Chemistry* open on his knees and a highlighter in his fist. On the dresser the Sanyo’s rabbit ears are spread in a V, one tip wrapped in foil, over a converter box with the government coupon sticker still on it, and the picture under them breaks into blocks now and then around the Fox logo. Theo comes in at five to, in the blazer, with the teacup level in one hand and a bag of kettle corn in the other, and installs Hollis on the dresser beside the antenna. “Keep the ears off him,” he says. “He’s a sensitive.”
Margot arrives with the clock, a legal pad under her arm, takes Doug’s desk chair and turns it until she faces the screen at an angle of disapproval. “I’m here,” she announces, “for the torture.”
“Dude,” says Doug, warmly. “You like it?”
“I have watched every season, Douglas, in the interest of scholarship. I am Scandinavian. We study what we disapprove of very closely.”
“He’s a real guy, dude,” Doug says, to the room, about the man on the screen. “Like a guy who *exists*.”

“I know him,” says Theo, on the floor against Jack’s shin, with the kettle corn between his knees. “I once waited forty minutes at the Ivy for him to finish a Cobb salad. A Thursday, the booth by the hedge. He ate the egg last, and he did not look up.”
“You *waited* for Jack Bauer,” Doug breathes.
“I waited for a salad. He was its guest.”
“Where were you standing?” Margot says.
“Near the hedge,” says Theo.

On the Sanyo a man is shot in the shoulder, keeps running, and opens a door with the same arm. “That’s a through-and-through to the deltoid,” Kevin says, to the orgo. “He’s carrying a rifle with it. I’d give him a sling and a lawyer.”
“It’s a flesh wound, dude,” says Doug.

“There’s no such thing, Douglas,” Margot says. “It’s a euphemism for a wound the speaker hasn’t had to look at.” She uncrosses her ankles. “You understand what this program is. It is the bedtime story of the Bush years. The world is dangerous, the grown-ups have it handled, and the grown-ups may do anything, because the clock is ticking. Justice Scalia asked a room full of judges whether they would convict Jack Bauer.”
“Would they?” Doug says. “Would *you*, dude?”

“That is not a question, Douglas, it’s a trap with a theme song.” She turns her chair a degree toward Jack. “And the bomb never ticks. That’s the fraud. In life no one knows there is a bomb, no one knows who knows where it is, and a man in a chair will say anything to make the chair stop, so you spend your night chasing a lie to a parking structure.”
“Okay,” Jack says. “The bomb doesn’t tick. I give you the bomb.”
“I accept the bomb.”

“But watch Doug.” On the bed Doug has stopped chewing and is following the screen with his entire face. “They’re not watching for the chair. They’re watching because somebody in there does the hard thing and pays for it. He loses somebody every season. He doesn’t get a parade. He never gets to feel clean. Where I’m from, the cavalry never came. You got a letter. I’m not defending the chair. The Church says torture is evil. Full stop. It’s in the Catechism.”

“I have read the Catechism, Costigan, in the interest of scholarship.” Margot regards him. “That is the most sympathetic thing anyone has ever said in defense of this program, and I want it noted that you did not defend waterboarding.”
“Noted by who?” says Doug.
“By me, Douglas. I note everything.”

In the next lull Kevin’s BlackBerry lights on his knee, twice, and the second time he turns it face-down on the orgo. “Clare’s going Saturday,” he tells the room, as though it had been asked. “The Walk for Life. In San Francisco. Newman’s sending the van.” He looks at his highlighter. “I said I’d go.”
“What’s the Walk for Life?” Doug asks.
“Thousands of people in San Francisco. Everybody gets a sign.” Kevin turns the highlighter over. “Is a march a date?”
“A march is a date for people who can’t dance,” Margot says.
“I can dance.”
“Demonstrate.”
“I can dance in principle,” says Kevin. Margot looks at him once, level and not unkind, and goes back to the screen.

On the Sanyo Jack Bauer puts a man against a stairwell wall and a knife into the outside of his thigh, and the man slides down the cinderblock with an expression of operatic finality. Kevin, quietly, from the bed: “That’s not where the femoral artery is.”
Doug goes over sideways onto the mattress. Margot puts the legal pad over her face, and her shoulders go. Theo applauds on his own knee, once. “Doctor,” he says.

A commercial comes on for a floor cleaner, in a kitchen of astonishing cleanliness. Theo takes a handful of kettle corn and holds it. “We could have watched in the Fishbowl,” he says to the handful, lightly. “Delaney would have let us have the second hour.”

On the bed Kevin looks up from the orgo, sweeps the textbook off the end of his mattress and pats the blanket twice, and Jack sits down on the corner of it. Theo’s eyes stay on him past the end of the sentence, and go back to the screen, and the second hour starts.

Theo’s eyes rest on Jack a moment past the joke. Then he eats his kettle corn.

response: Theo takes the bag, and the second hour, and the look, and keeps hold of the look until the man on the Sanyo has finished with the telephone.

s04.slug: MONDAY · 11:52 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL, THE 3RD–4TH LANDING
body: The bulb on the landing lives in a wire cage, and it makes a cage of the light too: a grid of shadow thrown down the concrete steps and up the cinderblock, with Jack sitting in the middle of it on the third step from the top, in his socks. Behind him, up half a flight and down the hall, 412 is dark and Theo is asleep in it, with Hollis in his teacup on the nightstand keeping the watch. Jack opened the landing window when he came out. It goes six inches and no further, and the night comes in through the gap, eucalyptus and wet asphalt and a fine rain that hasn’t made up its mind, ticking now and again on the sill.

He came out here at half past eleven because 412 is too small for a phone that lights up. He knows what it looks like, a man taking his phone into a stairwell at midnight. It’s been two nights. Marisol has been a very large town for two nights, and he has the RAZR in both hands between his knees, shut, like something he’s keeping warm.
It goes, and goes again, and again — three texts crawling in one behind the other on the RAZR’s little screen, a line at a time.

body: Then the little screen says *New Picture Msg*, and then nothing, for so long that he looks up at the bulb. The RAZR takes its time with pictures. It drinks them through a straw. When this one comes it arrives as a gray stamp in the corner of the screen, a square of pale shapes the size of a postage stamp that won’t hold still, and he tilts it toward the cage of light until the grain settles. He doesn’t open it. The three lines sit over it like a cover letter.

The others have come as if she couldn’t wait. This one waited. She took it at one in the afternoon and carried it around Burbank all day, through whatever a fitting is and whatever comes after a fitting, and at eight minutes to midnight she decided.

Out on the sill the rain stops ticking and comes down, heavy, the first real rain of the week, loud on the glass and blowing in through the gap in a cold spray across the landing and his socks. He doesn’t get up to close the window. His thumb is on the button.

choices.text: *Look at it, all of it. Answer her.*
choices.key: You opened the picture she sat on for eleven hours, and told her yes.
response: He opens it.

A fitting room: he works that out first, from the pins. A three-way mirror, the tall kind, with a row of pins stuck in the frame of the middle panel and the end of a rolling rack hung with garment bags. She’s standing in the middle of it with the white phone held up at her collarbone, her thumb on it in the glass, and the two side panels have taken her and turned her, so that she’s there three times over — once facing him, once from each side — and in the left-hand glass is the long line of her back, nape to heel, which no picture has ever given him, because she has always been the one holding the camera.

And the dress is coming off. Not off: coming off, caught on its way down — pale silk, not white, slipped from her shoulders and fallen nearly the whole way, pooled at her ankles, one bare foot lifted to step out of it. Every picture she has sent him she has held still for. In this one she’s moving. He can practically hear the silk go.

Her chin is level. Her mouth is open a little, as if she was about to say something and stopped to hear what he’d say first. She’s asking. Every picture she has sent him before this one already knew its answer. This one doesn’t: this is her not holding still, not arranged, caught halfway out of something, and the question on her face is whether he wants that one too. She must have had five minutes, somebody gone down the hall for pins, and she took a picture of herself asking him, and then she carried it eleven hours to see if she still wanted to ask.
He sits on the step with the phone close to his face and wants her so badly, so exactly, that it puts him back against the cinderblock. He doesn’t look away from it. He answers it.

Whatever she was asking him at one o’clock this afternoon, in whatever room in Burbank, she can ask him with her face. He’d rather have the face. He has wanted to see her face for two days more than he has wanted almost anything, and a picture of it the size of a stamp, under a cage, at midnight, is the wrong size.
He answers the captions instead, one key at a time.

He holds the button down. The RAZR asks him if he’s sure. He is. *Erased.* The square is gone and the menu closes up over the place where it was, and the question isn’t gone at all. He can still see the foot. He can still see her chin. He has the one look, and that’s all he’s going to have, and he can tell already it’s going to be plenty.
He looks at the two question marks for a long time. Then he sends her the one true thing he can.

body: Thursday the south wall of Morro 1100 was full of sun. Today it’s a sheet of gray with water going down it, floor to ceiling, shuddering a little in the gusts, and what comes through it is the light at the bottom of a pool. A third of the hall has stayed in bed. The rest have brought the storm in with them on their shoes.

Up in the back row the corner seat under the exit sign is empty, with nothing on it. No book keeping a place; no hood; no feet up on the seat in front. It’s folded up. Jack takes the seat beside it and puts *Oceanography 1* on his own knees.

Fenner comes on at eleven in the Tevas — in January, in this — with the coffee, and because of the third that stayed home he takes roll by pairs, off a sheet, not looking up. “Thirty-nine. Forty. Forty-one.”
“Half,” Jack says.
Fenner looks up at the back row over the coffee, at the folded seat and the one beside it.
“She says to tell you she’s drowning in Beverly Hills.”
“Not for drowning,” says Fenner, and makes his mark, and calls forty-two.
It’s exactly how Skye said he’d say it, Thursday, doing Fenner’s Texas in the back row, and Jack has to look down at his book.
Two rows down a girl in a crew sweatshirt brings her phone up at the angle that’s meant to look like checking the time, and points it at the back row. At the corner seat. The phone goes down.
Fenner does tides. Ten minutes into them the RAZR goes in Jack’s pocket, and he opens it under the lip of the fold-down desk.

s06.slug: TUESDAY · 3:52 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE BASEMENT
body: Three of the eight washers work, and all three are going — one of them with a sneaker in it, by the sound, knocking to be let out — and under them the vending machines hum in a key of their own. Jack has come down to feed another quarter to the end dryer, where his load has been going since three, when every phone in the basement goes off at once: the girl at washer two, the guy asleep on the bench by the change machine, his own RAZR in his jeans. Res Life, the second alert of the day. Funnel clouds reported over Las Olas. All residents to the lowest floor.

He’s on the lowest floor already. In five minutes the lowest floor is the entire building, and the stairs behind it are solid people, coming down in shower shoes and comforters, and there is no going up them against the current even if a man wanted to.

Priya comes down first, in a Res Life polo over flannel pajama pants, with a flashlight, a laminated roster on a clipboard and a whistle on a lanyard she has been waiting since August to use. At the foot of the stairs she uses it. Behind her three hundred and ten residents of Delgado Hall come down into a room built for eight washers, six dryers, two vending machines and the old upright against the wall, the one with the dead F that nobody in the building admits to playing, and they fill it to the walls and sit on the floor and on the machines and on each other’s coats.

“Away from the window wells,” Priya says, walking the room with the flashlight like a lifeguard. “Away from the glass. Sit. On the floor, please, not on the folding chairs, the folding chairs fold. Pruitt, get off the change machine.”

Jack stays where he is, at the dryer end, and sits down on the concrete with his back against his own load going round. Lena comes down with Laney among the second floor. He sees the top of her head in the stairwell first and then the rest of her, the gray cardigan over a T-shirt, her phone in her hand, and the two of them take the folding table at the far end by the piano, because it’s the last flat thing in the room, and sit up on it with their knees up. He turns around and reads Priya’s laminated sign about the quarters.

The rest of the fourth floor washes up around him. Doug has a family-size bag of Funyuns and the calm of someone who planned for exactly this. Margot is on top of a washer that works, holding her watch up toward the window well, where the rain is going sideways against the glass, timing the gusts for reasons she declines to share. Theo comes down nearly last with Hollis in his teacup and the teacup inside a stainless salad bowl from the fourth-floor kitchen, carried level in both hands. “Shock absorption,” he says, and takes the top of Dryer 3. From up there he looks down the room at the table by the piano, and the table by the piano is very interested in its phones.
Doug holds the Funyuns out to Margot. “For the end times.”
“The window wells are below grade,” Margot says. “If the creek comes up, we’re the aquarium.”
Doug takes the bag back and holds it a little closer.
“What’s it up to?” Jack asks her.
Margot looks at the second hand. “A gust every forty seconds. I was enjoying this ten minutes ago. I’ve stopped.”
Theo leans down off Dryer 3 with the bowl in his lap. “If the building comes down, Costigan, you save the egg,” he says. “I’m a legacy. They’ll find another one of me.”
“Hollis first,” Jack says. “Then the Funyuns. Then you.”
“That’s the correct order.” Theo settles back against the wall. “I’d shake on it, but I’m holding a life.”

Over their heads the wind gets into the window wells and makes a sound in them like a bottle being blown across, low and then higher, and the rain comes in under the edge of the frame on the far wall and runs down the cinder block in a dark stripe, and the room watches it run.

The storm kept Kevin from the 12:10, so he has the day’s first reading up on his BlackBerry and reads it to the six people within reach of his voice, and in a basement in a tornado warning it turns out to be a reasonable thing to do. Samuel at Jesse’s house with his horn of oil; the sons brought out one at a time, the tall one first. *Not as man sees does God see, because man sees the appearance but the LORD looks into the heart.*
Doug wants to know if David gets the girl.
“Several,” Kevin says, and scrolls on.

The power goes at 4:12. It goes all at once, the fluorescents and the vending machines and the three washers, which wind down in the dark with their loads slopping to a stop, and everybody says *whoa* on one note. Then the phones start coming up all over the room, one lit from the next, little blue squares at chest height, the way the candles go at the Easter Vigil, back from the one flame through the dark church.
For a moment after that the room is quiet, listening to the wind find the window wells.
At the far end a phone buzzes, close to somebody’s hand, and Lena answers it, low. “Hey. No, I’m fine. We’re in the basement.”

On the other end there’s a voice too small to be words. She listens to it. Jack knows from her own voice who it is; he has heard it across the lounge and on the stairs, the voice she uses for one person, slower at the ends, with all the argument taken out of it. In Julian’s song there’s a verse where the gardener doesn’t argue with her or explain anything, he only says her name, and Jack sits very still on the concrete in the dark until the verse has gone by.
Priya’s flashlight comes on at the foot of the stairs and swings across the room, over the machines and the faces, and finds her roster.

response: He stays on the floor with his back against the dryer, still warm, and waits for the dark to get shapes in it. It does, a little at a time. The pipes along the ceiling. The white bulk of the washers. Theo up on Dryer 3 with both hands on the rim of the salad bowl. Margot’s watch face, lit green when she presses the button. And at the far end the folding table by the piano, with two shapes on it, and one of them with a phone at her ear.
He looks at the dryers.

response: He gets up and steps over legs to the foot of the stairs, and Priya, who has the flashlight in one hand and the whistle in the other in case of further developments, gives him the clipboard without a word. He reads the fourth floor off it in her light. Answers come back out of the dark from all over the room: *here*, *yo*, *present*, somebody’s *ma’am*.
“Pruitt,” he reads.
“Present,” says Doug, from somewhere near the Funyuns.
“Pruitt, are you sure?”
Kevin laughs in the dark, one bark, unmistakably his. Jack reads the rest of the fourth floor and the third, and hands the clipboard back before the second.

choices.text: *Hold your phone up for Priya’s roster.*
response: He opens the RAZR and holds it up over the laminate so Priya can check off the third floor by its little light while her flashlight covers the stairs. It’s enough light for a clipboard. She goes down the names with her pen, fast, lips moving, and doesn’t miss one.
When she’s done she clicks the pen. “Costigan,” Priya says, “you’re a credit to the floor.”
She has never said it before. He’d bet money she denies it.

s07.slug: TUESDAY · 4:21 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE BASEMENT — THE LAUNDRY ROOM
body: The fluorescents come back in a row of stutters down the ceiling, and the basement squints. For nine minutes his eyes have been wherever the dark put them, and when the light comes they’re down the length of the room, past the washers and the heads and Theo’s salad bowl, on the folding table by the piano — and Lena is looking back. Her phone is shut in her lap, both hands over it. The light is the ugly light of a basement, flat and green and too much of it, and it shows him everything: the cardigan pulled closed, her hair coming down, the rain still on her boots.
He looks away first. He looks at the drain in the floor by his shoe until the vending machines have shuddered back on.

The all-clear comes at half past, and the news comes down the stairs ahead of it, phone to phone, from somebody’s roommate who knows somebody on Trigo: a tornado. A small one. It touched down in Las Olas and took a carport off a house on Trigo — Trigo, where he was shoveling sand at nine o’clock yesterday morning with an egg in his other hand — and a fence, and put trees down across Del Playa, and that’s all anybody knows. Priya reads the all-clear off her own phone at the foot of the stairs, and everybody gets up off the floor and starts back up in the order they came down, slower, talking about the carport.

He has the end dryer open by then, and both hands in it, feeling a load he already knows is wet. Laney goes up with Lena, a hand at her back on the first step, and he hears Lena’s boots go up the stairs among all the others; he’d know them on any stair in the building. Theo goes up with the salad bowl held out in front of him at the height of a ring bearer’s pillow, and says in passing, to Jack, “Hollis has been through a great deal,” and keeps going, and on the stairs he stands aside for no one, because the egg has right of way. Doug takes the Funyuns. Margot climbs down off her washer and tells Kevin the worst gust came at 4:17, and Kevin holds the stairwell door for her.
At the foot of the stairs Kevin looks back. “You coming?”
“Laundry,” Jack says, and Kevin takes that and follows Margot up.
Jack stays for his laundry.

The dryer stopped when the power did, and the clothes are warm and damp together, a heavy wet heat, with his gray Mooney T-shirt on top. Something buzzes in his jeans and quits; he has both hands in the drum. He has three quarters, and Priya’s sign says four, and he stands there with the door open and does the arithmetic. It comes out to about half his jeans.

With the building gone the room goes back to what it always is: warm lint, somebody’s dryer sheets, that sweet chemical smell that gets into the stairwell and up as far as the second floor, the washers ticking as they cool, the rain blowing in sheets across the window wells up by the ceiling. At the far end the folding table is a folding table again, with a gum wrapper on it and a wet ring where somebody set down a can.
Footsteps on the stairs, coming down quick. Flats. Laney comes around the turn by herself.
She hasn’t brought a basket.
She stops on the bottom step with one hand on the rail and waits there long enough that he thinks she might have come for something else, a hair tie, an earring, and might go back up without it.
“You made the bartender turn the music down,” she says. “In Sully’s. On a playoff Saturday.”
He waits for the threat. With Laney there’s usually a threat.
“I saw your face,” Laney says. “Saturday. After.”
“I was yelling,” he says. “That’s the face.”
“After,” Laney says.

She comes across the room to him, around the washers, over the Funyun crumbs where Doug sat, her flats leaving small wet prints from the stairs, and stops near enough to see what’s in the drum. She has a Pi Lam sweatshirt on with the sleeves pulled down over her hands, and she looks smaller than she does at a party. He wouldn’t have thought that was possible.
“If this is about Saturday,” he says, “she’s in L.A. till tomorrow. You can tell her yourself.”

“She brought me bells,” Laney says. “I’m keeping them. I’m not sorry, and I’m a little sorry.” She pushes her sleeves up, and they fall back down over her hands. “What the hell are you doing, fireman?”
He opens his mouth, and she doesn’t let him have it.

“No. I’ve been saving this, and I came down here for it, so you can hold your wet shirt and listen.” She finds her fingers inside the sleeve to count on. “The first weekend back, there’s a video. A girl with a sign at an airport, and you in it, and six thousand people watching you kiss her. I know, because I watched the second floor watch it. It went door to door before the vending machines were stocked. Then the little box on Facebook. *In a relationship.* By Sunday night. You hadn’t been back a whole day.”

Another finger. “Then you’re never anywhere. Kenzie Rourke says you come in the side door at Mass and leave at the blessing. You walk past the Fishbowl like it’s a crime scene. You sat down here for half an hour today with your back to the room, reading Priya’s sign about the quarters. Nobody reads that sign. You could recite it at a funeral.”

“And Saturday.” She doesn’t count that one. “You want to yell at me in Sully’s, go ahead. I had about half of it coming. Six days I walked past you like furniture. You said so, and the bar heard you say so, and fine. But she was sitting right there with the rope in her hands. And when you came back in at the end, she saw you in the door and she got her jacket. Fourth quarter. Saints winning.” Laney’s voice doesn’t go up. It goes flat. “She doesn’t come down to the lounge. She does the twelve-ten and class and Newman and then she’s just gone. She’s sitting right there on her own bed in our room and I can’t find her.”
She takes a breath through her nose. “And you look *great*. That’s the part. You look like a commercial for a truck.”
Her sleeve falls back down over her hand.
“And if you so much as learn a girl’s name tonight, I will have you killed, fireman, and I will wear white to the service, and everybody will say how well I’m holding up.”
She lets him hear it. Upstairs somebody is running a bath, and the water goes along the ceiling over their heads in the old pipes.
“I was there,” he says.
“One night,” Laney says. “That was the whole instruction.”

He has the three quarters in one hand and the Mooney shirt in the other, warm and wet, and he can feel it coming up in him from somewhere older than Saturday and lower than the back of his neck. It has been sitting there since November, unasked.

When it comes, it comes too loud for the room. Too loud for any room this size.

response: “I’m doing laundry, Laney.” He holds up the shirt, wet, to prove it.

She doesn’t laugh. She doesn’t do the thing with one eyebrow that means she’ll laugh later, at a party, telling it. She stands there in her flats on the concrete with her sleeves over her hands and waits, and the joke hangs in the warm air by the dryers and doesn’t hold, and what’s under it comes up through it while he’s still looking for something to put on top.
“She’d moved on in a week, Laney. I don’t know what the right timeframe is for that stuff, but I’m pretty sure she’d have waited more than a week if she was interested.”

Laney’s hand goes to the dryer door and stays there.

body: She doesn’t come back at him. He has watched her come back at people since August, and he braces for it, and it doesn’t come. Her arms come down, and her sleeves come down over her hands again, and she takes half a step closer instead, so that he has to look at her, and when she says it there’s no Dallas on it anywhere, nothing for a party; she’s asking him.
“She was really upset, Jack, and she didn’t have anyone.”
It should help. It makes it worse.
“Yeah, well. So was I.”

He hears it in the room after he’s said it, in the warm air with the lint, with the washers ticking and the rain going over the window wells, and it doesn’t sound like a thing he’d say. It sounds like something he has been saying for two months with his mouth shut, and now somebody has heard it.
Laney’s hand comes off the dryer. She opens her mouth, and whatever is in it, she doesn’t say.
He leaves her standing there. He goes past her and around the washers and up the stairs with the three quarters still in his fist and his clothes still in the drum, and behind him the room is quiet.

The east stairwell smells like wet concrete and the storm, and the steps are tracked with everybody’s rain. Doors bang open above and below him, people going back to their rooms, somebody’s TV through a fire door with the weather on it, a girl on the landing telling her mother about the carport on Trigo like she was there. The second-floor door is wedged open, and through it the long hall runs down past 217 with its door shut, and he goes on by.

Priya is coming down against the traffic with a roll of paper towels and a fresh laminate for the window well, and she stops him with the flashlight, which is off. “Costigan. There’s a dryer down there with your stuff in it.”
“I know,” he says, and keeps going, and she lets him.
Somewhere past the third floor he notices he’s taking the stairs two at a time, and stops, with his hand on the rail and his heart going like he ran it.
It’s the first time he’s said it to anyone. Not Danny. Not Osei. Not Skye.

He didn’t know it had words until it was out. He’d have said, if anybody had asked him, that he was good — that she was happy, and he was happy, and it was January. It’s out now. It’s in a laundry room with Laney Price, in Laney Price’s keeping, and there’s no putting it back.
He opens his hand. The three quarters are slick with sweat, and there are three red half-moons in his palm where his nails were.

There’s lint on his sleeve, and his sneakers are wet from the basement floor, and he’s left the Mooney shirt down there with the rest of it, a dryer’s worth of clothes in the basement. They can stay there.
It was both of them already, since Saturday. Now it’s for good: the far end of rooms and the near side of doors, nothing rude about it, and not one more thing for either of them to keep.
He takes the rest of the stairs one at a time.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven. The ninth at nine at the Anchor, with an agenda on an index card: pie, no questions. Sunday night she came out of my room with her laptop and went past me without a word. Since Sunday she hasn’t said a word to me. At the Haiti table she met Skye, and gave a hundred dollars to the clipboard. Wednesday night in the lounge she was keeping it short with Theo, for a nod. Then, to me, without turning her head: ‘Night.’ At Sully’s Skye brought her a present. She wore her own bells. She gave Skye advice, and I told her I’ve seen her work. Then she took a shot at Skye, and Skye was handling it, and I didn’t let her. I’ve never yelled at Laney before. The whole bar heard. Tuesday, after the storm, she came back down to the laundry room by herself, with a list: the airport, the status, Sully’s, the jacket, me. She asked what I’m doing. I told her the truth, which I haven’t told anybody. Then I left her standing there. I’m done with that room. Both of them.

body: At 4:31 he was in the laundry room. At 4:47 he was on the stairs.

On the screen a map of Massachusetts has gone red from the outside in, and a man at a glass desk is using the word *stunning* for what has to be the fourth time. They’ve called it. A Republican state senator from a town called Wrentham, a guy nobody in the lounge had heard of at Christmas, has taken Ted Kennedy’s seat, fifty-two to forty-seven, and the man at the desk keeps saying *Kennedy’s seat* as if a church had burned down.

Doug is on the floor in front of the set in his sleeping bag. “My cousin in Worcester called it,” he tells the room. “Like, in November. He has a lot of opinions. He has a truck. He says it’s all the truck.”
Kevin, on the arm of the couch, thumbing his BlackBerry: “They’re saying forty-one. He’s the forty-first vote.”
“Of what?” says Doug.
“Of no.”
Margot is in the armchair with her Docs up on the coffee table. “A filibuster-proof majority,” she says, “that lasted from a swearing-in to a special election. I’d like that on a sampler.”
The man on the screen says *Kennedy* again. It’s six past six. Jack is due at the Anchor at seven.
Eight minutes later he’s in the bus shelter on Ocean Road, with the rain blowing in under the roof at his shins, and he calls her back.
“Massachusetts,” Skye says. “Go.”

She’s out. He can hear it: a corridor somewhere with a vending machine in it, a door with a pneumatic sigh, and her voice half a step up and racing on whatever she has been drinking out of paper cups since ten this morning. “I’ve been in a booth for seven hours breathing at myself, and the sound guy had CNN on his laptop with the sound off the whole afternoon, and everybody in that building looks like their dog died, and I need somebody to explain to me why. Go.”
He starts. He gets to the sixty votes.
“Wait. Are you walking?”
“I’m at a bus stop.”

“Walk.” A machine clunks something into a tray on her end. “I can hear you standing. You’re standing in a little glass box like a bus-stop Republican. New rule: you explain your politics while you walk, and I tell you why you’re wrong, and at the end you’ve had exercise.”
“Since when is that a rule?”
“Since now. I’ve been told when to breathe all day. I’m making rules.” A paper cup crunches. “Call me back when you’re walking.”
And she hangs up on him.

He knows that voice. Half a step up and racing is what she sounds like at the end of a day of being told when to breathe; he heard it for an hour in the Saab the night she drove him to Burbank to be her cousin from Ohio. It isn’t a bit. It’s what’s under the bit, and what it wants is somebody to argue with who won’t tell her when. So he doesn’t argue about the rule.
He rides the 11 to the harbor with the phone in his fist and the bus windows streaming, and gets off at the foot of the wharf, and puts his hood up, and calls her back.
“I’m walking.”
“I can hear it. You squelch. Go.”

So he walks the wharf, out toward the end of it with the RAZR inside his hood against his ear, past the bait shack and the shut fish market and the boats knocking in their slips, and he explains Massachusetts.

Ted Kennedy had that seat for forty-seven years. Since he died in August a friend of his has been keeping it warm, and it’s been one of the sixty — the number you need in the Senate to stop the other side talking a bill to death — and on Christmas Eve the health-care bill went through the Senate with sixty exactly, not one to spare. The minute Brown is sworn in it’s fifty-nine. He’s the forty-first no.
“So you’re happy,” Skye says.
“I’m glad the bill’s in trouble. I’m not glad about him.”
“Explain the difference. Walk faster, you slow down when it gets complicated.”

He walks faster. The bill, the way the Senate wrote it, pays for abortion — not straight out; there’s a deal in it Ben Nelson got that’s supposed to wall the money off, and the bishops say the wall’s made of paper. The House passed a real wall, the Stupak amendment, and now the two bills have to become one bill, and he would rather have no bill than the Senate’s. “That part I’m glad about.”
“And the man.”

“The man’s pro-choice. Sort of. The Massachusetts kind.” A gull goes up off a piling in front of him, complaining. “And Massachusetts already has its own health care, basically everybody covered — Romney’s — and Brown voted for it. So the guy who’s going to stop the national one voted for the state one, and he’s pro-choice, and he won driving around in a truck. I’m not getting the bumper sticker.”
“You don’t have a bumper. You have a bus pass.”
“I have a very nice bus pass.”

“Okay. My turn.” She’s walking too; he can hear heels on concrete, the big hollow echo of a parking structure. “Massachusetts didn’t vote against health care, Jack. You just told me — they have health care. They voted against being taken for granted. She ran like she’d already won. She called the baseball guy a Yankees fan.”
“Curt Schilling.”

“I don’t know who that is and I’m offended on his behalf.” A car door, a long way off in the garage, booms. “And the people who write the checks for those ads didn’t think they had to show up for this one. I know those people. I’ve been to their houses. They have a lot of art about the poor.”
He laughs. She doesn’t give him time to recover.
“And he posed *nude*. In *Cosmo*.”
“He posed nude in *Cosmo* and won a Senate seat,” Skye says. “I posted a surfboard and I’m on probation.”

He laughs so loud, out there on the wharf in the rain, that a man hosing down a fish-cleaning table under a work light looks up from it. She laughs with him, and then, not quite laughing: “I mean it. Corinne sent me an email with a *subject line*.”
“What was the subject line?”
“*Going forward*. In italics.” A door hisses on her end. “Oh — and Tomás texted. Your tornado went down Del Playa. It took Sol’s swing.”
“Took it?”
“*Took* it. Like Oz. Sol’s devastated. She’s been sitting on the steps all afternoon in mourning. Tomás found one of the chains in the neighbor’s yard.” The heels stop. “It was a good swing.”
He’s at the end of the wharf by then, at the rail, with the harbor black and jumping under the lights and the rain coming across it in curtains. The left chain squeaked every time it went back.
“It was a good swing,” he says.

He turns around and starts back up the wharf, because it’s twenty to seven, and because she isn’t finished, and because he isn’t either. Somewhere in a parking garage in Burbank she’s walking in circles so she can keep arguing, and he is soaked to the knees on a wharf in a storm doing the same, and he could not tell you one thing that’s wrong.

choices.text: “They didn’t vote for him. They voted against being told.”
choices.key: Walking the wharf in the storm, you told Skye Massachusetts voted against being told.
response: “That’s *mine*,” Skye says. “That’s what I said.”
“You said it worse.”

“I said it *first*.” She gives him nothing; she laughs at him instead, past the bait shack and the fish market, and makes him say it again so she can tell him what’s wrong with it, which is that it’s hers.

By the time he gets to the Anchor’s back door he’s wet through to the skin, the Carhartt dark to the elbows, the shirt over his arm wet under it, his sneakers full, and he’s still losing. “I have to go wash dishes.”
“Say goodbye like a senator.”

He does it in the voice of every man who ever stood at a podium in a blue tie — he thanks the good people of the Commonwealth, he thanks his wife and his truck — and she shrieks in the parking garage, and hangs up on him for the second time tonight.

choices.text: “You’re right about Massachusetts. It already had its own.”
choices.key: Walking the wharf in the storm, you gave Skye Massachusetts: it already had its own health care.
response: There’s a silence on her end, in the garage, long enough that he takes the phone away from his ear to see if he’s lost her. He hasn’t. It’s her being pleased.
“Say it again at the next pier,” she says.

He says it again at the next pier, and at the next one, because she asks, back up the wharf in the rain, until he’s standing at the Anchor’s back door wet to the skin, with water coming off the eave onto his hood, and she still wants it once more.
“Goodbye like a senator.”
“I yield the remainder of my time,” Jack says.
“*Motion carried*,” says Skye, and she’s gone.

choices.text: “*Cosmo*’s a magazine. You’re a Facebook.”
choices.key: Walking the wharf in the storm, you told Skye *Cosmo*’s a magazine and she’s a Facebook.
response: “I’m a *Facebook*?” She’s delighted. He can hear the heels start up again. “I’m going to put that on my headstone. Under the other thing. *Beloved daughter. Also a Facebook.*”
“You can’t argue with it.”

“I can argue with anything, I’m from Los Angeles.” And she does, back up the wharf: that a magazine is a Facebook with staples, that the centerfold was 1982 and she was 2010 and that’s worse for *him*, that he’s only winning because he’s outside.
He gets to the Anchor’s back door wet through to the skin and leans on the dumpster lid to get his breath back. “I have to go wash dishes.”
“Goodbye like a senator.”
“The gentleman from Ohio has to go wash dishes.”

“The gentleman from Ohio is *excused*,” Skye says, and she’s gone, and he stands under the eave a little longer with the phone against his chest and the rain coming off the gutter in a rope in front of him.

body: The storm has been on the windows since the afternoon. From the dish pit Jack can see it only as water going down the glass, with the wharf lights run into it, the red and the green and the long yellow of the bait shack, none of them where they were an hour ago. Tuesday is half-price chowder. Tonight the chowder has two harbor guys in boots at the back booth and one man at the counter, and the rest of the Anchor is a lot of empty vinyl.

Rudy’s nephew has the flat-top, a tall kid in a hairnet who turns each patty over as though it might file a complaint. Rudy is at his meeting until half past eight; Gloria mentions it like the soup, as something the kitchen does on Tuesdays. She is at the pass topping off ketchup bottles through a funnel, with the pencil through her bun, and when Jack comes out of the back with the first bus tub, his hair still wet and his sneakers going *squish* on the mat, she says:
“How was Saturday?” He opens his mouth. “Don’t tell me,” she says, and caps the ketchup.

At the far stool Ray Ochoa has his Tuesday meatloaf and his black coffee and the windbreaker he wears in all weathers, zipped to the throat. Rudy’s transistor has come down off its shelf over the pass and stands on the counter at his elbow, tuned to a news station out of Los Angeles, and the news is Massachusetts: a Republican has taken Ted Kennedy’s seat, and the Democrat is conceding in a level voice, thanking a long list of people. Jack has already explained Massachusetts once today, in the rain, and the radio is getting it more or less the way he did.
Ray hasn’t touched his coffee. He is looking at the window, where the lights run, and he says it to the glass.
“Nobody out on the Point in this,” he says. “I hope.”
Jack tops off the mug from the pot. Ray lifts a hand from the counter in thanks and goes back to the window.

By eight the harbor guys have gone out into it in a body, and the night turns into dishes: four racks, then eight, then a wall of them down the steel. Jack is still halfway through a smile that started on the wharf, and he feeds the Hobart with it on. The steam smells of lemon rinse aid and hot plastic racks, and he works inside it with his sleeves shoved up.

s10.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:14 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE LOBBY
body: The only light in the lobby is coming out of the Fishbowl. Somebody has left CNN on in there with the sound off, and the blue of it fills the glass box and spills out through the wall onto the linoleum as far as the mailboxes, and the rest of the lobby is the exit signs and the rain running down the big front windows.

He hasn’t slept. He got off at one with his hands pruned from the Hobart and lay in the dark in 412 with the rain on the window, and every time he got near sleep he was back in a basement saying it. At ten past three he gave it up and came down in the Carhartt and his sneakers with no socks, with four quarters in his fist for a Coke. The east stairs were wet all the way down from everybody’s shoes. On the lobby bulletin board somebody has pinned a new flyer over the Haiti one, TORNADO??? in marker and a phone number for a guy on Trigo who lost his carport and wants to know if anyone has pictures, and under the front doors the rain has come in a dark tongue across the mat.
Marcus is asleep at the front desk with his cheek on a chemistry textbook, a page of hexagons under his ear and the highlighter still uncapped in his hand.
Lena is in the Fishbowl.

She’s by herself on the couch nearest the set, with her knees drawn up under the gray cardigan and her phone shut in her lap, and the screen is all over her: blue on her face, blue on her hands, blue in the rain still on the window behind her. Across the bottom of the picture the red band says BREAKING — STRONG AFTERSHOCK HITS HAITI — 6.1, and above it, without any sound, a man in a suit is talking to a map.
She hasn’t seen him. He’s standing in the dark of the lobby twenty feet from the glass with the quarters going warm in his hand.

choices.text: *Go in.*
choices.key: At three in the morning you went into the Fishbowl and sat with Lena and the earthquake.
response: He puts the quarters in his pocket and crosses the linoleum, past Marcus and his hexagons, and pulls the glass door. It sticks at the bottom. She hears it, and doesn’t turn her head.

choices.text: *Stand at the glass.*
choices.key: At three in the morning you stood at the Fishbowl glass. Lena turned the news off and sat in the dark.
response: He goes as far as the glass and stops there, close enough to touch it, with the lobby dark behind him and nothing between him and her but the wall and the blue.

On the screen they’ve gone to a picture of the map again, with a red dot where the coast bends, and then to a phone held up in a street somewhere in the dark, people moving through the frame too fast to see. Lena watches it with her chin on her knees. Then something makes her turn her head, the movement or the cold off the glass or nothing, and she sees him.
She looks at him through the wall. He can’t tell how long. Long enough that he knows he should do something with his hands and doesn’t.

She reaches down the couch for the remote. She points it at the set as if at a man across a room, to say *you*, and the picture goes, and the blue goes with it, and the Fishbowl is a glass box in the dark with a girl in it.

She doesn’t get up. She sits on in the dark, with her knees up and the remote in her hand, and the only light on her now is the red of the exit sign over the front doors, a little of it, along one cheek.

choices.text: *Keep walking.*
choices.key: At three in the morning you saw Lena alone in the Fishbowl and kept walking.
response: He keeps walking, past the glass and the blue and the back of her head, to the basement door, and goes down.

Down there the washers are dark and the floor is dry again and the room still smells of the storm, and the Coke machine takes his four quarters and thinks about it, and drops two cans into the tray, one after the other, *clunk, clunk*. He stands there with one in each hand. It’s the first thing that has gone his way since Saturday, and there’s nobody to tell.

When he comes back up the Fishbowl is dark. The set is off. The couch is empty, the cushion she was on still pressed down at one end, and the remote is lying on the arm of the couch, squared to the edge of it, exactly, the way she lines up a pencil with a book.
He stands at the glass with a Coke in each hand going cold against his palms.

s10a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:40 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL, THE 3RD–4TH LANDING
body: Rain is coming down the landing window so thick that the lamps on the walk below are only smears of yellow, and the glass hums in its frame every time the wind leans on that side of the building. He doesn’t open it. He sits on the third step from the top with his back against the cinderblock, cold through the Carhartt.

body.text: *You can stop.* It goes around in him with the rain, in her voice, with her hand on the door frame, and it doesn’t get any clearer for going around.
Behind his eyes the Fishbowl is still a box of dark in the dark lobby, and the red of the exit sign along one side of her face, and the remote in her hand.
The two Cokes are on the step beside him, unopened, sweating onto the concrete. He keeps seeing the remote on the arm of the couch, lined up with the edge.

body: His own pack has been in the inside pocket of the Carhartt since Saturday, against his ribs, with the lighter. In the other pocket, the tin, which isn’t his: eleven.
Saturday’s, on the church steps, was the first since New Year’s.

It starts in the hands, then the chest, an itch with an opinion; it came up the stairs behind him from the lobby, and it has been sitting on the step beside him since. Upstairs, through the fire door, somebody’s alarm clock goes off for no reason and gets slapped quiet.
His hand is already inside the jacket. He can feel the cellophane under his fingers, the corner of the pack, the lighter.

choices.text: *Light one.*
response: He goes up the last flight to the roof door and pushes it open on the night and props it with the toe of his sneaker. The rain comes in, onto his knees and the top step. He sits in the gap with the door against his foot and lights one of his own with his back to the wind, and smokes it in the noise of the roof, the water pouring off the parapet a few yards away, and doesn’t taste it much.
When it’s down to the filter he pinches it out wet and puts the end in his pocket. His jeans are soaked to the thigh.

choices.text: *Put it back.*
response: He pushes the pack back down into the inside pocket, below the lighter, and zips the Carhartt to the throat over it. Then he sits on the step with his hands outside the jacket, one on each knee, and keeps them there, and listens to the rain do what it’s doing to the window until the hum in the glass is just a sound again.

choices.text: *Open the tin. Count them.*
response: He takes the tin out of the other pocket instead and opens it on his knee, under the bad light. RELIQUARY on the lid. He counts them with one finger. Each one is a place.
Eleven.
He shuts it. The lid makes its small flat sound, and he holds the tin closed in his hand a while before it goes back.

s10b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:16 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: Inside the glass it’s warmer, and close, and quiet: the hum the set makes with the sound off, the rain on the window behind the couches. He sits down at the far end of her couch, on the arm side, with the Carhartt still zipped. She doesn’t look away from the screen.
“Six-point-one,” she says. “They’re saying.”

It’s morning there. The light in the footage is gray and new, and it comes from somebody’s phone, held up and shaking, in a street in Port-au-Prince full of people who were asleep in it. They come up off the road in one movement. A woman in a nightgown with a little boy on her hip runs straight into the middle of the street, away from a wall; a man goes down on his knees in the dust with both hands up, and stays there; a girl in a school sweater is screaming a name, over and over. On one side of the street there are no buildings at all anymore, only a long slope of broken concrete with rebar coming out of it like weeds, and as the phone swings across it the dust comes up off it a second time. Then the picture jerks and drops and is somebody’s feet running, and then a man in a studio again, with a map.
She watches all of it with her knees up and her arms around them and her phone shut in the hollow of her lap.

He watches it too. It’s what there is to do with his eyes. He knows where she is on the couch without looking: the cardigan, a T-shirt under it, her hair still damp at the ends and twisted up in a knot with a pencil pushed through it, out of habit, with nothing to write on. Her feet are bare, tucked under the hem of the cardigan, and one ankle shows, and he looks at the map. It’s the first time since the back hall at Sully’s that he’s been in a room with her and nobody else, and the room is a glass box in a dark lobby at three in the morning, and nothing is happening in it but the end of the world somewhere else.

The rain gets heavier on the window and eases off. On the screen they show the street again from the start, and then a reporter in a flak vest standing in front of a tent city in the dark, and then the map with the red dot. Under her breath, so low it’s mostly the shape of it, she’s praying. He catches enough of it, once, when the set goes quiet between segments — *never was it known* — to know which one.

He has his own. He says a Hail Mary at the woman in the nightgown, and another at the man on his knees in the road, with his mouth shut, the way Nonna taught him for sirens: fast, no frills, like a man throwing a rope. Two prayers going up off one couch.
Her eyes don’t come off the screen.
“They sleep in the street because the street’s the one thing left that can’t fall on them,” she says, low and fast, to the screen, “and now the street won’t hold still either. Lord have mercy.”
“You don’t have to sit with me.”
“I know.”

He stays. He sits there with his hands between his knees and watches the people in Haiti come up out of the street over and over, and every few minutes the red band along the bottom crawls the same sentence past, and the man with the map points to the same place on the coast. The couch is the length it is.

The cable box under the set says 3:31 when she puts her feet down. She stands, and pulls the cardigan closed across her front with both hands and holds it there, and goes to the glass door, and gets it open, and turns around with her hand still on it.
“Whatever you’re doing, Jack — you can stop.”
“Doing what?”
Her hand finds the door frame, and holds it, and lets go.

He’s alone in there with the set. He goes back over the week looking for it. The last pew. The far end of every room he couldn’t keep out of. He has kept out of her way as hard as a man can. He doesn’t know what else she could mean.

On the screen the phone comes up in the gray street again, shaking, and the woman in the nightgown runs out into the middle of the road with the little boy on her hip, from the same doorway, the same way, the boy’s arm around her neck, and the dust comes up behind them off the broken concrete again.

The pipes go first: the far shower working its way toward hot, one knock and a long pause and two more, and under them the rain on the window toward the Grove, steady since Monday night. Jack got to sleep a little after five, on top of the blanket in his clothes, with the RAZR rising and falling on his chest. The light at the blind is gray and has no source.
The knock on the door isn’t Kevin’s. Kevin knocks twice, politely, and says his own name. This is three, flat, and nothing after it.

Theo is already up, which Theo is not before ten without a court order. He’s at the desk in the wine-colored robe with the Sigma Rho pin on the blotter and Hollis on the nightstand in his cup, and he gets to the door first.

Laney is in the doorway with no face on. That’s the first thing, and then it’s the freckles: across the bridge of her nose and out over both cheekbones, copper on porcelain, hundreds of them, and Jack, up on one elbow with the crease of the blanket still in his cheek, has known her since August and has never seen a single one. Her hand comes up flat over her nose and the near cheek, and stays there, and comes down again. It’s no use, and she seems to know it. Her hair is in a rubber band. She holds her phone in both hands at her breastbone, as she held the root beer at Sully’s before she set it down without drinking.
She looks at Jack once. There’s no ice in it and no “Night.” Then she looks at Theo.
Jack lies back down and looks at the ceiling.
“Theodore. Hall.”

Theo, who has an opinion on every doorway he has ever stood in, has none. He starts, “Give me a second to —” and she says, “No,” and he lifts Hollis off the nightstand in both hands and goes out barefoot in the robe, with the teacup held in front of him at the level of his heart.
It is the first time Jack has seen Laney Price come looking for Theo since the Sunday of the status. Since then she has addressed him by text in the third person and, at Sully’s, in the imperative.

The door shuts behind them. Jack doesn’t get up to listen; there would be nothing to hear. The hall carpet takes whatever’s said, and what’s left is the pipes, knocking along the wall toward the far shower. On the nightstand a pale ring marks where the cup has sat all week.
He sits on the edge of the bed with one boot on and the other in his hand. The rain goes on. Ten minutes by the RAZR.

Theo comes back alone, with Hollis, and shuts the door with his heel. He sets the cup down in its ring and dresses without a word, and Jack has never seen that: Theo doing up a cuff link with nothing to say about it. Now he ties the tie, undoes it, ties it again. He puts the Rolex on over the wrong sleeve and moves it. To free both hands for the cuffs he hangs his umbrella by its crook from the post of Jack’s bed, and then the cup is back in his palms, level, and he’s at the door with his back to the room.
“Costigan.” Too casual. “Where are you at eleven?”
“Tonight?” Jack says. “Here. I owe Hale three pages.”
“Here,” Theo says, and nods twice, briskly. “Hollis likes to know where everyone is. He keeps a ledger. It’s mostly dining hall hours.”

He goes. It is another minute before Jack sees the umbrella still hanging from his bedpost, black and enormous, dripping onto the blanket. Theo, who held it over the cup on Sunday and not over himself, has gone out into Wednesday’s rain with the cup and without it.

Jack is pulling on the second boot when he sees his desk chair. His clothes are on it: the gray Mooney T-shirt, his other flannel, the jeans, three undershirts and the socks, folded in thirds with the edges lined up, the socks in pairs. He picks up the flannel. It smells of the basement, sweet and chemical, and of warm lint. He puts it on.
