body: It has been raining on Delgado since Monday night, steadily, with conviction, and the Saab is at the curb in it with the top down. The seats are dark with water. There’s water standing in the cupholders. Skye is behind the wheel in a soaked gray hoodie with the hood back and sunglasses on — sunglasses, at twenty to five on a January afternoon in a storm — and she’s laughing at him before he’s through the door.

She drove up the 101 from Burbank with the top up as far as the Rincon, she tells him later, and put it down there for the last ten miles because she missed weather. Los Angeles doesn’t have weather. Los Angeles has a forecast.

He makes it to the curb. She’s out of the car and around the hood before he can get to the door of it, and she takes his face in her two wet hands and kisses him on the sidewalk in front of Delgado Hall, in the rain, under every window on that side of the building, long enough that the rain gets into it — into his collar, into the corners of her mouth — and she laughs into it and keeps going.
“Three nights,” she says, when she’s done. “You look like you’ve been in a basement.”
“I was.”
“Tomás said.”

Then she peels the hoodie off over her head right there on the sidewalk, and under it is his flannel. She digs in the breast pocket of it and comes out with one mint, off a pillow somebody important was going to sleep on, and presents it to him on her flat palm in the rain like a ring. “It guarded your shirt,” she says. “It never left its post.”

Then she peels the flannel off too and hands it to him, wet on the outside and warm on the inside and smelling of a hotel — some soap he couldn’t afford the name of. “It hated it,” she says. “It sat in a parking garage and thought about you. *Avatar* won everything. Everybody told me they saw it in 3-D. A man who owns part of a *studio* told me he saw it in 3-D like he was telling me he’d been to Lourdes.”

body.text: “Now,” she says. “Open it.” She means here, now, on the curb in the rain. “I want to see what you think. I didn’t know what you’d think.” So he gets the RAZR out under the flannel and opens it — three of her, the size of a stamp, with rain beading on the screen — and she doesn’t look at the phone once. She watches his face. Whatever his face does, she sees it before he has a word ready — he watches her see it — and he puts the phone in his pocket, and she takes hold of the front of his shirt for a second, hard.

“‘I saw it,’” she quotes at him. “Period. Like a receipt.” “I said I’d tell you to your face,” he says. “So tell me.” He tells her, on the curb in the rain: that he looked once and erased it, because once was going to be plenty, and it was. She looks at him through the rain running down her sunglasses. “Plenty,” she says, as if she’s trying it on. Whatever else she decides about it, she keeps. She takes his hand, and pulls him toward the car.
“You said yes,” she says. “I said yes.” She pushes the sunglasses up into her wet hair to watch him say it again, so he says it again, and she looks pleased enough to be dangerous.

body: “Get in,” she says. “We need field data.”

She takes Seacliff out to the end of it with the top down and the wipers going for no reason, since most of the rain is coming in over the top of the windshield. The dirt lot at the end of Seacliff is a brown lake with a sawhorse across the mouth of it and a county sign zip-tied to the sawhorse — BEACH CLOSED · NO WATER CONTACT — and she noses the Saab up to the sawhorse and kills the engine, and they sit in the open car in the rain in the last of the light, and look.

The Point isn’t there. Not the Point he’s seen from this lot, with the long lines walking in out of the west and bending at the reef the way she drew them on his legal pad, peeling off it one after another, neat as a zipper. There aren’t any lines. The sea is brown a mile out, and from the reef to the sand it’s white, all of it, standing up and falling over in every direction, and the noise of it comes up the bluff and into the car and doesn’t stop for breath.
“The reef’s still aiming it,” Jack says. “Everything at the same rocks. It’s just all arriving at once.”
Skye has her chin on the top of the door, her wet hair stuck to her cheek. “It’s not breaking where it does,” she says. “It’s breaking everywhere.”

Up the bluff from the lot the old Light stands white and shut, and below it the low wall runs along the edge, and at the end of the wall is the white cross. Somebody leaves flowers there on Sundays — Tomás said so — and Sunday’s are gone, torn off by yesterday’s wind. All that’s left at the foot of the cross is a length of kitchen string snagged on the fence wire, standing straight out sideways in the gale.
“Somebody’s going to be sad Sunday,” Skye says.
Jack looks up at the crossbar, at the rain running down the white paint over the name.
She starts the car.

The bluff road runs north along the top of everything, and she takes it with the top down in the downpour, and puts her iPod on the dash and turns it up as far as the Saab goes — something big and bright and synthesized, a song built for driving fast in the sun — and they drive it in the rain. The heater’s on full, roaring at their shins, cooking their ankles while the rest of them drowns. He doesn’t know the words. He screams it anyway, whatever the words are, and so does she, with the rain coming straight down into the car and into their open mouths, and the eucalyptus going by black and streaming on the right, and on the left the sea white out to the edge of what they can see. She drives with one hand and puts the other up into the rain, palm open, catching it. Her hair is plastered flat. Her mascara is a ruin. She has never looked better and she would kill him for saying so, and he says so, at the top of his lungs, over the song, and she screams with laughter and doesn’t take her hand down.

At a turnout above the water she pulls off and stops, and turns the music down, and leaves the engine running with the heater going. The rain comes down on them. Her thumb is going on the wheel, back and forth, one small stroke. He knows the thumb. It goes like that before she says the thing she means instead of the thing she’s good at; it went like that in the Saab on Mission Street on Saturday, before *I can tell there’s a rest*. He shuts up and lets it get there.

“Tuesday,” she says, “you didn’t answer me for an hour and forty-three minutes. I counted. And then you called me from a bus shelter and you were funnier than you’ve ever been in your life.” She’s looking at the water, not at him. “You were *so* funny, Jack.”
He doesn’t say anything.
“Something happened Tuesday that isn’t the tornado.”

The rain on the hood. The heater. He doesn’t answer her, and she doesn’t make him; she lets it be. Her thumb stops on the wheel. She reaches over and wipes the rain off his eyebrow with it, the left one, across the scar, and then she leans over him and gets the white phone out of the glove box, where it has been staying dry.

She reaches up and clicks on the little map light over the mirror, and holds the phone out at arm’s length with its back to them, because that’s the only way, and leans in against him, wet from her hair to her shoes, and takes it. Takes three. She shades the screen with her hand and looks, and turns it around to show him the one she wants: the two of them in an open car in a storm in the dark, grainy, lit gold from above, her hair stuck to her head and her mouth wide open laughing at the lens, and him turned toward her instead of it, laughing too, with rain in his mouth. The drops show up in the light as white streaks, falling through the picture. It doesn’t look like January. It looks like two people who haven’t heard about January.
“Can I?” she says.

s12a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:20 PM · THE SAAB, SEACLIFF ROAD
body: The top is up at last; it went up at the light at Seacliff and Ocean with the motor whining. With it up the Saab is a small loud room — rain drumming on the canvas a foot over their heads, the wipers going, the heater going, the two of them steaming in it like laundry. Her hair is in wet strings. His jeans are a different color than they were this morning.
Skye has been up since four, in Studio City. She tells him so with her head back on the headrest and her eyes shut, at a red light, with her hand on the gearshift.

“Come home with me,” she says. “I’ll make you cereal.” She rolls her head on the headrest to look at him. “I had plans for you. I had a *list*. And my body vetoed them. My body has filed a formal objection, and it’s going to be asleep by nine whether I like it or not.”

It’s a good line, and it’s a line. Under it her eyes have gone to the middle distance and stayed there, as they do after three days of being looked at, and he knows this one: when she gets funny about being tired she needs a small room with just him in it, where she doesn’t have to be anything.
He has three pages due on Hale’s table at one o’clock tomorrow, and he hasn’t written a word of them.
The light goes green. She doesn’t go. She waits, with her hand on the shift, for him.

choices.text: *Go home with her.*
choices.cue: Skye will hold on to that.

response: She puts the car in gear before he’s finished saying yes, and goes through the green that’s already gone yellow, and takes the turn for Las Olas one-handed, with the other hand on his knee in case he thinks about getting out.

choices.text: “Giorgio’s. You can watch me write.”
choices.key: Wednesday night you took Skye to Giorgio’s and wrote your pages while she read you waves.
response: Giorgio’s on a storm night is a back booth and an empty room, and nobody in Giorgio’s has ever wanted her to be anything but hungry.
“I love watching people work,” she says, and puts it in gear. “It’s my favorite thing nobody pays me for.”
She swings them back toward Mission Street with the wipers on high, and at the next light she leans over and steals the flannel back off his knee.

s12b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:10 PM · DEL PLAYA, THE HOUSE
body: The porch smells of Sol’s cigarette and wet boards. Sol is on the top step under the eave in a man’s raincoat three sizes too big, with her knees up and her old camera in her lap, smoking like a widow. She doesn’t get up. She lifts the cigarette at Skye, and at Jack, and puts it back in her mouth.

Over her head, in the porch ceiling, there are two hooks with nothing on them. A length of chain still hangs from the left one, swaying in the wind off the water, tapping the post. The other chain is lying on the boards by the door in a wet coil where Tomás dropped it, the last link at the end of it pulled open. Where the swing went is anybody’s guess. The ocean, Skye says Tomás thinks.
Skye crouches on the step beside Sol and puts her arm around the raincoat. “We’ll get another swing.”
“There isn’t another swing,” says Sol.

The screen door bangs and Tomás puts his head out — wet hair, board shorts in January, a mixing bowl of something in one hand. He looks at the rain. He looks at Jack. “Point’s closed, bro,” he says, and takes his bowl back inside.

Her room is cold, and the window over the mattress is black with the water somewhere down below it. She takes the wet flannel off him and hangs it over the heater, and makes cereal for dinner in two mixing bowls, because every bowl in the house is in the sink — Honey Nut Cheerios, with the last of Tomás’s milk — and they eat it sitting on her mattress with their backs against the wall, in dry sweats she finds for both of them, his too short in the leg. When the flannel is warm she puts it on over her T-shirt and pulls the cuffs down over her hands, and lies down across the mattress with her head in his lap.
His hand goes into her hair. It’s still damp at the roots, cold, and it smells like rain and somebody else’s shampoo.

She tells him the party. She does the man from the network — a tan like a good saddle, calls everybody *kid*, asked her four separate times whether she’d been thinking about her *brand* — and then she does the ficus, which is mostly a long and dignified silence with leaves in it, and which she says was the better conversationalist by a mile. She does Corinne two tables over mouthing *smile* at her across the ballroom, all teeth, like a woman warning somebody off a ledge. She does the bathroom: a woman in a gown on the phone to her mother in Encino, crying about a seating chart; two girls from a show she won’t name being very busy in the end stall; and her on the closed lid with her shoes off, the only one in there not working.

He laughs at the ficus, because the ficus is funny. He doesn’t laugh at the bathroom. That’s the one that isn’t a bit; he can hear the joke go out of her voice at *shoes off*, a half-second flat, and he puts his hand back in her hair and leaves it there.

“And you texted me about rain,” she says. She tips her head back in his lap to look up at him upside down. “Everybody in that hotel was talking about *Avatar*, and you sent me the weather in Marisol. I read it in the car on the way home. Twice.”
Her eyes close.
“Friday,” she says. “Conan’s last show. Here. On Tomás’s TV. I’m going to be awake for it. I am going to be so awake, Jack. I’m going to make popcorn and be sad about a man I’ve never met.”
“I’ll be here.”

“Good.” Her hand finds his knee through the flannel cuff and stays there. She’s on Corinne again by twenty to ten — Corinne’s email, Corinne’s subject line, how Corinne writes *per our conversation* about conversations that never happened — and she’s halfway into “and then she copied my *mother* on it, which is —” when the sentence just stops. He looks down. Her mouth is a little open and her breath has gone long and slow, and her hand has gone loose on his knee. Nine-forty, by the clock on her dresser, and she’s out, in the middle of a sentence about Corinne.

*My mother* is the one place her voice goes careful, every time. She says it fast and turns it into a joke before anybody can look at it, and he has never once asked. He sat through a lunch with Debbie and a legal pad and rules on it. He knows enough. What he knows tonight is that she fell asleep on the word, and it’s the first sentence all week she hasn’t had to finish.

choices.text: *Pull the blanket over her.*
response: He gets the blanket off the foot of the mattress without moving his knee, and brings it up over her to the chin. Then he works himself out from under her head, a little at a time, and puts the pillow where his lap was. She doesn’t wake. She pulls the blanket in under her chin with the cuff of his flannel and says something to the pillow that isn’t a word.

At a quarter to eleven Tomás drives him back to campus in the van, with two boards loose in the back rattling over every pothole on Del Playa and the wipers losing. Tomás doesn’t say a thing the length of Las Olas. At the Delgado curb he leans on the wheel and looks up through the windshield at the rain, and says his second sentence of the night, which is the same as his first. “Point’s closed, bro.”

choices.text: *Leave a note on her Oceanography book.*
response: Her pencil is in the gutter of *Oceanography 1*, on the floor by the mattress, where she’s been keeping the place at chapter four. He gets it without moving his knee and writes on the cover, small, in the corner where she’ll see it first.

At a quarter to eleven Tomás drives him back in the van, the boards in the back clattering every time they go over a dip, the wipers barely keeping a hole in the windshield. At the curb Tomás looks over at him for a while, a man weighing what ought to be said at a time like this, and says it. “Point’s closed, bro.”

choices.text: *Say goodnight to her asleep — out loud, in case.*
response: “Goodnight, Skye.”

He says it at a regular volume, to her face, in case some part of her is keeping track. Her eyelids don’t move. But her hand, loose on his knee, closes on a fold of his sweatpants and holds on, and doesn’t let go until he’s got the pillow under her head instead.

At a quarter to eleven Tomás drives him home in the van with the boards rattling in the back and the defroster losing, and doesn’t say anything until the Delgado curb. There he puts it in park and looks out at the rain coming down on the empty quad, personally let down by it. “Point’s closed, bro.”

body: Giorgio’s windows have run down to the sills with rain and steam, so that Mission Street outside is only a smear of red brake lights and the green cross on the pharmacy, and the light in here comes from the little lamps over the booths, low and orange on the checkered oilcloth. It’s nearly empty. Everybody with sense is home.

They have the back booth and a large pie, half pepperoni and half plain, because she’s a purist about nothing in the world but this. She sits sideways with her back against the wall and her wet sneakers up on the bench, in his flannel again, with *Oceanography 1* open on her knees. He has a Giorgio’s pen and a placemat — a map of Italy, the regions in five colors, a cartoon chef in a toque standing in Calabria where Nonna’s from — turned over to its blank side, because his legal pad is in 412 and the three pages are due at one.
Three pages on why you are wrong. Frankenstein; the trial; the girl they hang; the silence. He has to find the sentence that starts it.

“Welcome,” Skye says, in a voice like a carpeted hallway, “to Chapter Four.” She turns the book to an imaginary group behind her. “Please stay together. Please do not touch the waves. You are now standing in front of a wave. Notice the crest. Notice the trough. The trough is the low part. The artist has made the trough low as a comment on the human condition.” She turns a page. “If you’ll follow me into the next gallery, we’ll see what happens when a wave reaches shallow water. I won’t spoil it. It breaks. Press seven on your keypad for the gift shop.”
It’s the voice she does when she’s happy and doesn’t want to be caught at it. He’s heard it on the 101, giving the trucks their lives. He doesn’t tell her he knows. He writes.

He writes the first sentence and crosses it out. He writes the second. She goes on through the galleries — the period, the fetch, the wave of translation, which she says is the wave’s *late period*, when it stopped caring what critics thought — and he writes under it, a paragraph, then most of another, eating crusts off the plain half without looking. The rain keeps coming down the window beside them.

When he stops to read it over she leans across the pizza and reads it upside down. She reads slowly, with her lips almost moving. Then she puts one finger, greasy at the tip, on one sentence. Not the first. Not the clever one.
“That one,” she says. “That’s the one you actually think. The rest is you doing Hale.”
He looks at the sentence under her finger. It’s the one he almost didn’t write down.

She sits back against the wall and takes another slice, and folds it in half, New York, which she does to irritate the waiter. “Friday,” she says. “Conan’s last show. My house. I’m going to be awake for it.”
“Friday.”
“I’m going to make popcorn and cry about a man I’ve never met.” She points the slice at him. “You’re going to hold the bowl.”

choices.text: *Cross out everything but the true sentence.*
response: He draws a line through everything else, sentence by sentence, the clever one first, until there’s one sentence left alive in the middle of the placemat with Italy on the other side of it. Skye watches him do it with her chin on her hand.
“Brutal,” she says, approving. “You’re a butcher.”

At twenty to eleven she drops him at the Delgado curb with the top up and the wipers on high. “Three pages minus one sentence,” she says. “Don’t write anything you don’t think.” He goes up the steps with the placemat folded inside his jacket against the rain, and the one sentence on it.

choices.text: “Do the guide for this paragraph.”
response: She’s already in the voice; she lifts the placemat off the oilcloth like a piece in a case. “You are now standing in front of a young man who would like to be finished,” she says, in the carpet voice. “He has been standing here for some time. Notice the pen. Notice the crust he has not eaten. The artist —”
“Skye.”
“The artist would like to be left alone,” says the guide, and hands it back, and takes the crust.

At twenty to eleven she drops him at Delgado with the top up and the rain coming off the canvas. “Notice the pages,” she says, through the window, in the voice. “Notice that there are three of them. Tomorrow.” He goes up the steps with the placemat buttoned inside his jacket.

choices.text: *Fold the placemat and keep it.*
response: He folds it in four, carefully, along Italy’s borders, with the grease spot from her finger on the true sentence, and puts it in the inside pocket of the Carhartt. She watches him do it, and doesn’t say anything clever, and then she does.
“You’re keeping a placemat,” she says. “Of me being right.”
“That’s why.”

At twenty to eleven she drops him at the Delgado curb with the top up. He gets out into the rain with his hand on his jacket over the pocket, to keep it dry, and she leans across the passenger seat to the open door. “Write the rest of it like that one,” she says. And then he shuts the door on her, because it’s raining in on the seat.

s13.slug: WEDNESDAY · 10:50 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE 4TH-FLOOR LOUNGE — MEETING #2
body: The lounge door is propped open on its wedge, and the fluorescents come out through the gap and lay a white stripe down the hall carpet, the only lit thing on the floor. On the stairwell door behind him Priya’s laminate still has the pen underneath it: WEDGES ARE A LIFESTYLE. He has come up for hot water. The tap is in the vending alcove just inside the lounge door, the instant coffee is in the Carhartt, and Hale’s three pages are due at one tomorrow and he is nowhere near three. His jeans have not forgiven the rain.

He opens the door the rest of the way with his foot. Inside, a hand slaps the frame of the whiteboard and the board goes over on its swivel, end over end, a good deal faster than the swivel was built for: a white blur, a squeal of casters, and at the top of the turn, for half a second, upside down, the back of it goes past with a word on it in pink capitals, FACTS, underlined three times, the last line running off the edge. Then the other side comes round and rocks to a stop. USEFUL IDIOTS FOR CHRISTIAN NATIONALISM, and under it COSTIGAN | BROUSSARD in Margot’s marks, months old. The side he knows.

Theo has one hand on the frame and the other in his blazer pocket. Laney is on the window seat with her knees up and a pink marker in her fist, her face back on, lashes and lip, the copper hair brushed to a shine. Margot is in the armchair with a notebook open on her knee. Kevin is on the couch in plaid pajama pants and a quarter-zip, bolt upright, arms crossed, like a juror who has been told he can’t go home. On the coffee table, on a coaster, Hollis presides from his teacup.

Jack has seen these four in this room a hundred nights. He has never seen them sit up straight. And Laney and Theo are sharing a room with no third party to address each other through. Jack hasn’t seen that in ten days.
He looks at Theo, and at Kevin, and at Margot’s notebook. Not at the window seat.
“Costigan.” Theo’s voice is a half-step too warm, and the board is still rocking behind him. “Perfect timing. You’ve caught us.”
“Did the board just —”
“It’s on a swivel,” says Theo.
“It’s an excellent swivel,” says Margot, from behind the notebook.

“We’re planning Delaney’s nineteenth.” Theo is not going to stop now. “Valentine’s Day, which falls on a Sunday this year, a gift, because there’s no class on Sundays and everyone is already feeling a little bad about their lives. Agenda.” He holds up three fingers. “The cake, from the Vons on Mission, her name spelled correctly in writing. The guest list, fourteen, a crowd. And a theme.”
“Teal is a hostage situation,” Laney says from the window seat.
“Teal has been withdrawn.”

“I want real piping on the cake,” Laney says. “Not gel. Gel is for people who’ve given up. And I’m being surprised.” She does the face: hands to both cheeks, eyes wide, mouth a perfect O, held, and dropped like a window shade. “I’ve been practicing.”
“She is being surprised in committee,” says Margot.
“And Hollis,” Laney says. “On the guest list.”
“Hollis is staff.”
“Hollis is a *guest*, Theodore.”
“Hollis has abstained,” Theo says. “He’s an egg of principle.”
“I’d like it entered that I want a tiara,” says Laney. “A small one. Plastic. I’ll know.”
“The tiara is in the minutes.”
“The tiara is not in the minutes,” says Margot.
“It’s in the minutes,” says Theo. “In pencil.”
“Overlord took two years,” he adds, to Jack. “The beaches didn’t even have a theme.”
“That’s a lot of work for a sheet cake,” Jack says.
“It’s a very complicated sheet cake.”
“Sixty dollars,” Theo goes on. “Margot has proposed we spend all of it on a banner.”
“Banners are the oldest instrument of coercion,” Margot says. “I am on record against them. We are getting a banner.”
“Kev,” Jack says. “You okay?”

“I want it noted that I’m here under protest.” Kevin says it to the room at large, fast. “I was in bed. I have a quiz at eight a.m., I was in my bed with my quiz, and I was brought here, I was physically brought, and I think as a general principle that everybody should leave everybody alone.”
“Noted, sugar,” says Laney.
“I’m not on the committee,” Kevin tells Jack. “I’m the designated adult. Nobody asked.”
“Want me to say you’re excused?”
“There’s no mechanism,” Kevin says. “I checked.”
“What’s the notebook?” Jack says to Margot.
“Participant observation. I’m told it’s legitimate.”
“Of what?”
“That is what the notebook is for.”
“Theodore,” Laney says, to the room, “tell him the tap sticks.”
“The tap sticks, Costigan.”
“I heard her, Theo.”
“Tell him I know,” says Laney.
“Indirect discourse,” says Margot. “It’s in the literature.”
He gets his mug under the tap. The water begins, thread by thread, to fill it. Behind him four people and an egg go quiet in the manner of people pretending to have been in the middle of something.

choices.text: “Put me down for the theme. Pageant.”
response: Laney’s mouth goes, and comes back, and goes again, like a car trying to start in January. She looks hard at the ceiling and overrules it.
“Pageant,” Theo says, writing nothing down. “A theme with legs.”
“Seconded,” says Margot. “For the data. The motion carries over my objection.”
“Please don’t second anything,” Kevin says. Then, fast: “If there’s a theme, I’d like it calm. Tide pools.”
“Tide pools are a subcommittee,” says Theo. He turns to the window seat. “Delaney, you’ll need to leave the room for the vote.”
“I’m *in* the room, Theodore. I’m being surprised in it.”

Laney unfolds from the window seat and crosses to the door, and because the tap is beside the door, he’s in her way. She doesn’t go around. Her hand closes on his left arm above the elbow and squeezes, hard and quick, and lets go. “Night,” she says to the hall.
Kevin examines the ceiling tiles. Margot’s pen comes down on the page and goes up again without having written anything.

choices.text: “What’s going on with you two?”
response: “We’ve reconciled,” Theo says. “Over a principle.”
“Several,” says Laney.
“Name one.”
“The principle,” Theo says, “is that you don’t ask the committee what the committee is for.”
“I asked,” Kevin tells Jack. “They said it was a committee thing.”
“It was a long negotiation,” says Margot. “I took minutes.”

Laney is already up. She crosses to the door, and the tap is beside the door, and he is in her way; her hand closes on his right arm above the elbow, quick and hard, and lets go. “Night,” she says, to the hall, as if she had been saying it all along.
Kevin looks at the ceiling. Margot’s pen writes a letter, stops, and lays itself along the spine of the notebook.

choices.text: *Get your hot water and go.*
response: The tap gives him water at the speed of the Delgado plumbing, a thread, a drip, a thread, and the room waits him out in total silence. Theo’s hand stays on the frame of a board that has stopped rocking. Kevin studies the ceiling tiles above the couch. Margot’s pen hovers over the notebook, and hovers, and the page stays blank. On the coffee table Hollis watches with the serenity of the unhatched. Once, Theo opens his mouth, and Laney says, “Don’t,” without turning her head, and he closes it.

About halfway, Laney gets up off the window seat and crosses to the door, and has to stand there at his elbow, because the tap is next to the door and he is next to the tap. She waits. The mug fills a third of the way and stops. Starts. He puts in the coffee and stirs it with the wrong end of a pen.
When it’s full, she goes first. Her hand closes on his arm above the elbow, quick and hard, and lets go. “Night,” she says, and the hall carpet takes her flats.
He follows her out with the mug. At the door he looks back at the couch. “You’ll live, Kev.”
“That’s what they say to the ones who don’t,” says Kevin, to the ceiling. “I’d like it noted that this was worse than the quiz.”

s14.slug: THURSDAY · 12:20 AM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE PAGES, AND A HYPOTHETICAL
body: The rain on the window toward the Grove has gone steady and close, and under it, from Theo’s side of the room, comes Theo’s breathing, too even and too quiet to be a man asleep. Jack has the desk lamp bent down low over the legal pad so the light stays on his side of the divider. Hollis is on Theo’s nightstand in the teacup, catching a little of the lamp.

Three pages on why you are wrong. He has a page and a half, and an eraser worn down to the metal, and Theo’s blazer on the back of his own chair where Theo threw it at ten past eleven, because Theo’s chair has Hollis’s salad bowl on it. *Frankenstein* is open face down on the desk to the trial, the spine cracked white at the page where Victor says the tortures of the accused didn’t equal his. Jack has underlined that one so many times since last Thursday the paper’s gone soft.

Hale gave him the wrong side and the wrong side is winning. He spent Thursday telling the table Victor was right to keep his mouth shut, and now he’s up past midnight arguing against silence, against himself, and every sentence he writes for it is better than anything he said at the table last week.

body.text: The Giorgio’s placemat is taped to the top of page one, grease spot and all, with Calabria showing through from the back.

The placemat is folded in four in the Carhartt on the back of his chair, where he put it. He copied the one sentence out at the top of page one in his own hand, and he’s trying to write the rest like it.

body: He writes a sentence. He erases it. He writes it again, worse, and leaves it.
“How many pages,” Theo says from the dark, not a question.
“A page and a half.”

“Hale will smell it on you. He can smell a page and a half from the stairs. He once failed a Rhodes Scholar for a paragraph that was *trying*; I read it somewhere reputable.” The sheets go. “Hollis has a pledge breakfast at six-thirty and a chapter dinner at seven, and at midnight he is either a brother or an omelet, and I’d like to be awake for whichever.”
“You’ve been awake since Monday.”
“I’ve been awake since puberty,” Theo says. “Write your page and a half.”
Jack writes. Theo goes quiet over there, and the quiet goes on long enough that Jack has nearly finished a paragraph inside it.
The next thing out of the dark is a pitch.

“Hypothetically. I’m developing something. A man has a friend — a girl. Her boyfriend from home ends it. The man stays put. He has his own girl. He’s decent about it. A week later the friend is with a musician.”
Jack’s pencil has stopped. He doesn’t turn around. On the nightstand the egg sits in its cup.
“Question for the room,” Theo says. “Is the man hurt, or relieved?”
“That’s a terrible pitch.”
The bedsprings go as Theo turns over, toward him, toward the lamp. He doesn’t sit up.
“A man has a friend,” Theo says again, to the dark, exactly as before. “A week later she’s with a musician.” And then, quieter: “A week, Costigan.”

It lands somewhere under his ribs and sits there. He knows who the man is; Theo might as well have put up a photograph. *A week* is the word he used on Laney on Tuesday. It’s a common word. Wes, on All Souls. Julian by the middle of the month — she told him in the Grove, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs. He isn’t going to talk about any of that to the dark at midnight.
What he doesn’t know is why Theo Vance, who falls asleep when he decides to, is lying awake past midnight in the dark with an egg on his nightstand and a pitch he’s said twice.

choices.text: “Hurt. He’d be hurt. He’d tell everybody he wasn’t.”
choices.key: At midnight Theo pitched you a man whose friend was with somebody new in a week. You told him the man would be hurt.
response: “Hurt,” Jack says, to the legal pad. “He’d be hurt. He’d tell everybody he wasn’t.”
Nothing comes back out of the dark for so long that he thinks Theo has finally gone under.
“Good note,” Theo says, short, and turns back over to the wall.
Jack sits there with the pencil and the thing he just said, for the second time this week, to the second person. The second time is realer. He bends the lamp lower and goes back to Victor.

He finishes at ten past two. The last page is the easiest. He doesn’t trust it. He writes his name at the top of page one, and the class, and Hale’s name, and stops with the pencil on the line where the date goes.

choices.text: “The man should get a roommate who sleeps.”
choices.key: At midnight Theo pitched you a man whose friend was with somebody new in a week. You told him to get the man a roommate who sleeps.
response: “The man,” Jack says, “should get a roommate who sleeps.”
“The roommate has insomnia.” Theo settles back into his pillow, unbothered. “It’s a character trait. It gives him texture. Audiences respond to it.”
“Go to sleep, Theo.”

“I’m in development,” Theo says, and is quiet, and the quiet doesn’t sound like sleep either. Jack can feel him over there in the dark, waiting for a better answer, and he doesn’t give him one. He bends the lamp lower and goes back to Victor in the courtroom.

At ten past two Jack writes the last sentence of page three and doesn’t read it over. He turns back to page one and writes his name at the top, and the class, and stops on the line for the date with the pencil resting there, and can’t think, for the life of him, what it is.

choices.text: *Pretend to be asleep at the desk.*
choices.key: At midnight Theo pitched you a man whose friend was with somebody new in a week. You pretended to be asleep at your desk.
response: He puts his forehead down on his arm on the legal pad, and breathes slow, and lets the pencil roll out of his fingers to the edge of the desk.
From the dark: “You don’t erase in your sleep, Costigan.”

He doesn’t lift his head. Theo doesn’t say anything else. After a minute Jack hears him turn over toward the wall, and after another he sits up and picks up the pencil off the edge of the desk where it stopped, and erases, and goes on.

By ten past two he has three pages, and he gets them in order with the lamp bent low, and writes his name at the top of the first one and the class under it, and stops with the pencil on the space where the date goes and leaves it blank.

body: It rained all night, and in the morning it rains harder: the big one, the one the radio has been promising since Sunday, coming in off the Channel sideways, so that the eucalyptus along the Grove lean over and roar and let go of limbs onto the walk. The creek that runs dry under the Grove path eleven months of the year came up over the footbridge sometime before dawn and took the path with it. From the Delgado steps Jack can see the brown water going through the trees, fast, carrying bark.

He has Theo’s umbrella, because Theo hung it on Jack’s bedpost yesterday and hasn’t asked for it: black, enormous, a handle of real cane, and the name of a shop on a street in London stamped in gold on the strap.

Skye comes up the walk from the lot in a yellow fisherman’s slicker three sizes too big, the hood up and rain dripping off the end of her nose, carrying two coffees in a cardboard tray that is going soft in her hands. She gives him one. With the hand that’s free she takes the umbrella away from him, opens it over the two of them with a snap, and looks up into it.
“This is Ted’s,” she says. “He’s had this since he was fourteen. He used to fence people with it at wrap parties.”
“It’s ten minutes to Morro.”
“Not the way we’re going.” She hooks her arm through his under the umbrella and turns him, away from the Grove, toward the Lagoon. “I didn’t drive over here to drive. Walk. Explain.”

So they take the long way, out along the Lagoon, where the path runs on a low bank between the water and the bluff and they are the only two fools out on it. The Lagoon has come up over its reeds. The rain pocks it out to the far shore, and the wind off the ocean pushes little brown waves across it backwards, toward the dorms.

He starts where the case started, because that’s the only way he knows how to explain anything. A nonprofit called Citizens United made a movie in 2008, *Hillary: The Movie*, ninety minutes of people on camera saying she shouldn’t be president, and they wanted it on cable, on demand, during the primaries. And McCain-Feingold said no corporation could pay to put anything on TV or cable that named a candidate inside thirty days of a primary. “So it was a crime,” he says, “to show a movie.”
“A movie paid for by a corporation.”

“Everything’s paid for by a corporation. The *Times* is a corporation.” He has the coffee in one hand and her arm in the other, and he’s walking and talking at once, which is the point. “In ’04, Wisconsin Right to Life wanted to run an ad on the radio telling people to call their two senators about the judges. Just call them. And it was illegal, because it said the senators’ names inside the window. They had to go to the Supreme Court to be allowed to say two names on the radio. They won, in ’07. For that one ad.” A gust comes across the water and she leans the umbrella into it without breaking stride. “And the Church is a corporation. Your archbishop’s a corporation. Legally. The Roman Catholic Archbishop of Los Angeles, a corporation sole. One man in a miter, incorporated. The NAACP’s a corporation. Pop’s Local —” He hears where it’s going and goes anyway, because it’s true. “The UAW can spend now too. Same as anybody.”
Skye stops walking. Under the umbrella that means he stops too, or drowns.
“I’m a corporation, Jack,” she says. “I’ve been a corporation since I was twelve.”
“You’re a —”

“My mother incorporated me. Skylark Pictures, Inc.” She starts off again and he has to lunge to stay under. “She named me a bird with a tax ID. Every check I’ve ever earned goes to Skylark, and Skylark pays me an allowance, and Skylark has an accountant in Encino I’ve met twice. Skylark gave five hundred dollars to a city councilman once. I found out at Thanksgiving.” She drinks her coffee. “And Meridian writes checks to both parties every two years, so whoever wins takes the call. I’ve been to the dinners. They put the girl from the show at the middle table, by the flowers, so the donors can say they sat with Cassidy.”
The rain comes across the Lagoon in one long sheet and hits the umbrella loud as gravel.
“I know what money does in a room,” Skye says. “I’ve been the centerpiece.”

Water strings off the ribs of the umbrella all around them, and he looks down at the top of the yellow hood and doesn’t have anything for it. She said the last part at her own pitch, with nothing on it at all. He doesn’t fill the quiet.
“So who’s right?” he says.

“Stevens is right.” She looks up. “He’s eighty-nine. He’s the grandfather at Thanksgiving who’s right about everything, and everybody passes the potatoes over his head. He read part of it from the bench this morning. You don’t do that unless you want the room to hear you lose.”

And she does them, or her idea of them. “I’m making this part up,” she says, “every word.” In her version they’re an old married couple who have been fighting over the same thermostat for decades: one of them earnest and wounded, from Sacramento, a hand flat on his heart, cold in his own house and sure the thermostat deserves a hearing; the other small and bow-tied and ancient and perfectly sure, who has kept it at sixty-eight since Ford and would like it noted that a thermostat can’t vote. She plays the argument twice through, both sides, with her chin and the umbrella, and the wounded one loses both times.
He laughs so hard he lets go of her arm and walks out from under the umbrella into the rain, and she reels him back in by the Carhartt.

She hands him her coffee and gets the white phone out of the slicker, the opinion still up on it from bed, and holds it in under the umbrella, beaded with rain. “This part’s real,” she says. “I’m quoting.” And in Kennedy, chin up, reading off the wet glass with the umbrella handle pressed to her heart: “*If the First Amendment has any force, it prohibits Congress from fining or jailing citizens, or associations of citizens, for simply engaging in political speech.*”

She scrolls a long way down with her thumb. “Also real.” And Stevens, very slow, very old, from somewhere down around her collarbone: “*Corporations have no consciences, no beliefs, no feelings, no thoughts, no desires.*” The phone goes back in the slicker, and she takes her coffee back, and for a second she doesn’t do anybody.

At the Lagoon bridge the wind finds them. It comes straight up the outlet off the beach, and Theo’s umbrella goes inside out with a crack, every rib together, and tears half off its spokes and flaps over their heads, black and useless and pouring water onto them harder than the sky is. Skye looks up into the wreck of it. There’s no closing it now. She brings it down wrong side out, and puts it over her shoulder, and carries it off the far side of the bridge like a trophy.

They walk the rest of it under nothing. The rain gets down his collar and into his shoes, and her hood fills and spills, and he can’t leave the thing alone, because what he said was true and so is the other thing.

“Leo the Thirteenth,” he says. “Eighteen ninety-one. He says a handful of very rich men had laid a yoke on the poor that was hardly better than slavery. He says a worker has a right to band together with other workers, because on his own he hasn’t got a chance.” He wipes his face with a wet sleeve. It doesn’t help. “So the Local gets to talk. And Meridian gets to talk. And Exxon gets to talk more than both of them before lunch. And my father, who’s been laid off since June, gets a vote and a lawn sign.” He stops. “I just argued myself into a corner.”
“You did. I watched the whole thing.”
“I think it’s right. The law was wrong; they were right to throw it out.” He looks at the Lagoon. “And I hate it.”
“You go back and forth on Thomas More,” she says, pointing the dead umbrella at him. “Go back and forth on Kennedy. I like you when you’re losing.”
Up the last of the bank toward Morro she walks backward in front of him, the umbrella on her shoulder and her face turned up into the rain, and holds one hand out at him, palm up. Go.

choices.text: “If the Local can spend, so can Meridian. That’s fair.”
choices.key: Under one umbrella you told Skye that if the Local can spend, so can Meridian.
response: “If the Local can spend, so can Meridian,” Jack says. “That’s fair.”
“*Fair*,” Skye says, “is a word for people who’ve never seen the invoice.”

He opens his mouth and finds nothing in it. She watches him find nothing, and turns around and walks forwards again up the bank, the umbrella bouncing on her shoulder. “One for the corporation,” she says. “The corporation is very happy.”

choices.text: “You’ve been in the room. I haven’t.”
choices.key: Under one umbrella you gave Skye the point: she’s been in the room, and you haven’t.
response: “You’ve been in the room,” Jack says. “I haven’t.”
She stops on the path in the rain. Water runs off the point of the yellow hood in a string.
“Say that at the next bridge,” she says. “I want to hear it with an echo.”

She comes back down the two steps between them and puts her cold wet hand inside the open Carhartt, on his chest, over his heart, and leaves it there in the downpour while a gull goes over them sideways in the wind. Then she takes his arm again, and they go on up the hill like that, very slowly, as if Morro will wait.

response: “The problem isn’t the speech,” Jack says. “It’s that nobody’s poor enough to be in the room.”

She stops in the rain to look at him. The dead umbrella comes down off her shoulder and hangs from her hand, dripping on her sneakers, and she goes on looking at him, wet to the skin, until he has to look at the Lagoon.
“Nobody at those dinners was poor,” she says. “Not one person. Not even the waiters. The waiters were actors.” She takes his arm. “Put that in a paper. Don’t say I gave it to you.”

choices.text: “You’re a corporation that steals mints off pillows.”
choices.key: Under one umbrella you called Skye a corporation that steals mints off pillows.
response: “You’re a corporation,” Jack says, “that steals mints off pillows.”
“Allegedly.” And she’s Kennedy again, outraged, hand on the heart, on behalf of the mint. “*Mr. Costigan. The mint is an association of citizens.*”

Every twenty yards up the hill to Morro the mint gets another sentence of its defense — its long service, its freedom of association with the pillow, the chilling effect on mints everywhere — and at the doors his hands are too full of coffee to get them open, so she does it, with her hip, and the umbrella goes in first.

body: Rain runs down the south wall of Morro 1100 from the floor to the ceiling, so the light that gets through the glass is white and moving, and the two hundred people who came sit in the bowl of the hall like people at the bottom of a swimming pool.

They come in at the top as Fenner reaches the lectern, the slicker shedding water on every step, Jack soaked from the hair down and leaving prints, the dead umbrella over her shoulder. Fenner is in the Tevas, with the coffee. He looks up the stairs at the two of them over the microphone.
“Pair forty-one,” Fenner says, in the Texas. “You’re wet.”
“Field data,” Skye says.
Somebody in the middle rows laughs. Fenner drinks his coffee and puts up a slide of a wave.

In the corner seat under the exit sign she wrings the hood of the slicker out onto the floor, which is not allowed, and stands the umbrella in the aisle wrong side out, where it drips. His notebook is wet through at the edges. Fenner talks about fetch: how far the wind has blown over open water before it gets to you, and how the longer the run of ocean and the longer the storm, the bigger what comes ashore. She takes his pencil, and in his margin, small, under the date, she writes *you argue better wet*. She gives the pencil back, folds her hands on the desk, and is a model student at Fenner.

Two rows down, a boy in a crew hoodie has his phone up over his shoulder, the lens turned back up the rows toward the corner under the exit sign, his thumb on the screen. Jack sees the lens, and the thumb. The slide changes to a storm off Japan. The phone comes down into the boy’s lap, and beside Jack, Skye writes *fetch* in his margin and draws a box around it.

The storm comes into 302 as light. At the window end the glass is running white and bright and the eucalyptus outside is thrashing in it, so the long table looks wet at that end; at the door end, under the clock, there’s only the overhead fluorescent and the radiator.

He has been in the third-floor stairwell since ten to one, with his pages in a folder under his arm and the RAZR open in his hand to the clock. The stairwell window looks down on the Hollis steps, and from it he watched Julian walk her across from the Commons under a black umbrella, with her book bag on his own shoulder. At the door Julian’s hand was at the small of her back, and she went in.

He comes in a minute before Hale. Evan is at the door with the roster on a clipboard, taking pages and checking names, and Jack hands his over and Evan checks him off without looking up. She’s at the window end, the last chair, with her back to the glass; her pages are already on the stack, and her *Frankenstein* is lined up with the table edge and the pencil across it. He takes the door end, under the clock. Yusuf is in the corner with his coffee.

She didn’t look up when the door opened. Last week she looked up and went back to her page; this week the page is enough. He gets his own copy out and opens it to the trial, and the margins he wrote in October look like somebody else’s handwriting, a boy with opinions.

Caleb has his phone out under the table edge, turned toward Yusuf, and he says it at the volume of a man who thinks he’s being discreet. “Costigan’s on TwitPic. Drowned rat, back row, with a celebrity.”
Yusuf looks at the phone and then at his coffee. Jack sees the back of it, Caleb’s thumb on the screen, and not the picture.
At the window end Lena turns a page.
Hale comes in with the rain on his shoulders and takes the stack from Evan, and the roster with it, and sits down halfway along the side, where he has to turn his head for either end.

“Three pages each on why you are wrong,” he says. “I have read every first sentence on the stairs, which is as far as most editors go and further than most readers. Most of you have written three pages on why you are right, with a paragraph at the end in which you are briefly and decoratively wrong. That is not an argument. That is a fucking curtsy.” He lifts the stack and lets it drop on the table. “I shall now read you one sentence from each, of my choosing, which you will find instructive or humiliating, and I don’t mind which.”

Every time Hale reads a name that isn’t his or hers, Lena writes something in her margin, small, with the pencil out of her hair; every time he turns a page, Jack’s eyes go to the window end and come back to the table before they get there. It’s like keeping your hand out of a pocket. He has had a lot of practice at that this week.

He goes down the roster in no order Jack can see. He reads Caleb’s — *Victor’s fear of being thought mad is the only sane thing about him* — and says, “Hargrove, no,” and goes on. He reads a girl from the window side on the miniature in Justine’s pocket, and nods. He reads Yusuf’s — *Nobody in Geneva asked the servant what she saw* — and lays it face down without a word, gently.
He runs his finger down Evan’s list.
“Broussard,” Hale reads, in the Oxford voice, off the roster. “Magdalena T.”

It goes into Jack whole. The name, flat off a list, in English vowels that have never been near the Bastille, and the *T.* after them like a receipt. Hale reads it like a train time, and it doesn’t matter how it’s read. Jack sits under the clock with his hands on the table until the word has gone all the way through.
“Lena, please,” she says, evenly, from the window end.
Hale looks up from the list. “Lena. Forgive me. The registrar is a romantic.”
Caleb laughs, and finds out alone that it isn’t a laughing matter, and turns it into a cough. Evan looks down at his clipboard as if the registrar might be on it.
Hale finds her page in the stack and reads it out.

body.title: From Lena’s pages, read aloud
body.text: *There is a silence that isn’t cowardice: when the truth would only be one more thing taken from people who have already lost everything.*

body: Her hand goes up to the medal at her collar while he reads, and takes hold of it through the cardigan.
Jack sees the hand.
Hale lays the page down and is quiet a moment. “Miss Broussard has defended silence better than Victor ever managed,” he says. “Which is a terrible thing to be able to say about anyone.”

It goes past Jack close, the sentence, like a truck past a man walking the shoulder of 422. There are things he doesn’t think about. He’s good at it. He sits with his hands on the table and doesn’t think about them now, and at the window end her hand doesn’t move from her collar, and her eyes don’t move from Hale.
The rain goes across the window in a gust, and every pen at the table stays down.
“Costigan,” Hale says, and finds his.

He reads it the same way, flat, off the page. *A man who keeps quiet to save himself has already confessed; he’s only chosen the wrong confessor.* He looks down the table at the door end. “Mr. Costigan has prosecuted himself and won. Appeal denied.”

It’s strange to hear it read, his own sentence in that voice, in that room, with the rain going across the window behind her. It sounds smaller than it did at two in the morning. It sounds truer. Down the table Lena hasn’t looked at him; she’s looking at the page in Hale’s hand.
Then Hale turns his head toward the door end and leaves it there.
“Mr. Costigan. She has made your Thursday case against you, and made it better. Answer her.”

The table turns with him, one face at a time: Caleb, the window girls, Evan with his pen up, Yusuf over his coffee lid. At the window end her hand is still at her collar. She’s looking at Hale, and only at Hale, and the storm light is all down one side of her.

journal.title: The medal
journal.text: Lena’s medal was her grandmother’s; it came back to her mother in a plastic bag. When she’s working something out, her hand goes to it. At the Point in December. Thursday at Hale’s table, about Justine. Saturday in the hall at Sully’s, about the Fishbowl. Thursday at Hale’s table, while he read out her paper about keeping quiet.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. I told her what Danny asked about the third. If Pop won’t get out of the truck, she says, I get in. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. She asked if I asked Ma who the candle was for. No. You don’t. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks. I know what that means. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it. New Year’s Day I called her from the garage at the half, and she said, You called *me*. Saturday night she called the house — Ma answered and talked to her for ten minutes. Two hours on the kitchen phone, her mother’s cordless dying twice. Her grandmother made the christening gown for Luc in 1985; it rode out the storm in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. She had me be the priest so she could practice the promises. She thinks Binx doesn’t stop looking — he stops looking by himself. I told her Danny asked me something I can’t answer yet; she didn’t ask what. She asked how California was. ‘Come back, Youngstown.’ Two hours, and she never said Julian’s name. Lucille was baptized in the third quarter, and she didn’t get one word wrong. After that I called every night. Twelfth Night she got the baby in the king cake. Friday she said she hasn’t been fair to Julian, and she’s going to fix it. Sunday she landed: come find me tomorrow. Monday I couldn’t find her — not at 217, not at the twelve-ten. She came into Hale’s seminar a step behind him with a king cake, and the only chair left was next to mine. She was polite to me for fifteen minutes. Then Dido. Tuesday morning Julian put up a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late. She’s tagged. She’d said call me after. I didn’t. At the mailboxes she asked about my break, and I told her as far as Denver, and Ma’s words about the coffee. ‘Tell her I’m glad.’ The baptism was lovely. Tuesday night at St. Brendan’s she had the whole thing organized by half past eight, in a whisper, and put me on the table with Becca. When the TV said trapped she left the room. Julian went. It’s true, and he lets it stand. At the window end Lena’s pencil stops on the page.

Hale looks at him, and down the table at her, and back, and picks up the next page off the stack without a remark. The hour goes on without either of them in it. Caleb argues for madness for twenty minutes and loses.
When the chairs go back she’s the first one up. She goes out by the far door at the window end, so she never has to come down the table past him.
Her chair is pushed in. Her end of the table is bare, except for the light coming across it off the rain.

Hale sits back in his chair as if somebody has finally poured him a drink. “*There* he is.”

“Go on,” says Hale, and he goes on — Victor in the courtroom with the proof sitting in his own chair, the girl in the cart, every day he let it stand — and he wins it, he can feel the table come over to him a sentence at a time, Caleb nodding, Evan writing fast. At the window end Lena’s hand comes down off the medal to the table and lies there, flat, beside the book.
She says nothing for the rest of the hour. When the chairs go back she’s gone before Caleb has his bag zipped.
The chair at the window end is still pushed back from the table, with the storm light on the seat.

response: “I said what I wrote.”
He doesn’t say it again. Saying it again would mean saying it down the table, to her, and he’s had enough of the far end of things for one week.
Hale looks at him down the length of the table. “You wrote it beautifully,” he says. “You didn’t say it.” And he goes on to the next page.
At the window end the hand comes away from her collar, at some point in the next sentence; he doesn’t see when.
When the chairs go back she takes the far door, the long way to the stairs; it keeps her off his end of the table.
In the corner Yusuf sets his coffee down and looks at it.

response: “Some people,” Jack says, “are very good at keeping quiet.”
He means the back hall at Sully’s. He means whatever it was she had in her mouth and kept there, with the halftime show coming through the wall.
Her hand is still closed on the medal. She looks down the length of the table at him for the first time today.
“Yes,” she says. “Some people are.”
Caleb stops writing. Hale turns over the next page.

The big storm has driven everyone indoors, and forty umbrellas lie open on the tile along the radiators to drain, black and navy and one plaid, a flock come in out of the weather. On the table by the mailboxes, tied in twine and still damp from the courier’s bag, sits a stack of Thursday’s *Tide*.

body.title: The Tide — FRONT STAGE · by Margot Lindqvist
body.text: “There is no backstage,” Skye Callender told me, over pie, in a diner on the wharf. “There are just more stages.” Erving Goffman would call that a very backstage thing to say. Callender counts four selves on a weekday — five on Thursdays — and says her boyfriend is “the only person I’ve ever met who’s the same in every room.” Of his faith: “I believe *he* does. Those are different, and the second one is very attractive.” Asked to respond, the subject’s boyfriend said, “She’s right.” I have chosen to treat this as data.

body: At the far end of the mailboxes, Theo and Laney have arranged themselves, shoulders turned half toward each other and half toward the lobby, one hand each raised to chest height as if weighing something. They are speaking at the volume of people who would like to be heard in the back row.
“— and that’s why it’s so important, Theodore,” Laney is saying, to the middle of the room, “to have *all the facts* before you assume anything about anybody.”
“I couldn’t agree more, Delaney.” Theo lifts a finger. “*Communication.* It’s the bedrock.”

Then they see him. Both freeze mid-gesture, Theo’s finger up, Laney’s palm out flat in the air as if smoothing a very large tablecloth. They hold it for two full seconds. Then they go on, louder and worse.
“Which is *exactly* what I was saying,” Laney says.
“*Exactly,*” says Theo, louder still.
“Are you two okay?” Jack says.
“Never better,” says Theo.

Laney crosses to Jack in four brisk steps, holding out her umbrella: pink, a scalloped edge, a brass handle. “Take it.” She presses the handle into his hand. Then she turns on her heel, chin up, and says to nobody in particular, at a volume that reaches the street: “I’ll want that *back*.”
The stairwell door opens, and Lena comes through the lobby with her mailbox key held out in front of her and a folder under one arm. She has the gray cardigan on.
Theo turns from Laney and gives her a nod, a good one, exact, with the correct number of degrees, and a flat “Broussard.”
“Theo,” Lena says, and keeps going.

At her mailbox she turns the key and takes out a catalog and one envelope, shuts the little door and locks it, and that is the entire transaction. She does not look at Jack. He has turned to his own box, with his key in it and the little door open on nothing, and he stays turned that way until her step has gone back up the stairs.
Jack has watched Theo be charming to Lena for five months. He has never watched him be correct.
Behind him there is a small, wounded noise. Theo has his eyes shut. “Too many degrees.”
“Not a one,” Laney whispers, lit up like a marquee. “Perfect.”
“Dude.” Doug is on the bench by the radiators with his laptop on his knees and his socks steaming on the grate. “I’m doing the wall. As a public service.” He turns the screen so the lobby can see it.
