journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Nineteen on the solstice, four days early, under protest. Likes us. On the record. Lit a candle for research. Took Skye’s side about the rose. Goffman, 1956. Wrote TED in her notebook and underlined it. Gave to Partners In Health and sent the rest of us there — Farmer’s Catholic, sort of. Commented ‘Front stage.’ on my status. Wednesday night in the lounge, while Laney kept it short with Theo: keeping score. A page in her notebook says SKYE. Thursday at the Anchor she interviewed Skye for her column. She hated that it was good. Her column ran Thursday: ‘Front Stage.’ It’s good. I told her twice.

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. She looked. Wednesday, in Eli’s truck, I told her. She said she did everything right, and she did. ‘It just isn’t the thing, is it.’ She asked me to leave it up on Facebook till she’s told her mom at the table. Thursday at two she texted. Still praying for me — not a girlfriend thing, she says. At the twelve-ten she turned around across the aisle at the sign of peace and held out her hand. Then she held it out to Lena. At the airport, a week to the day: St. Raphael, for Nonna. Father Osei read the name at the twelve-ten, and she heard. Thanksgiving: told her mom at the table. Texted me first — happy Thanksgiving, praying for Nonna, taking it down now. Then she did. The Immaculate Conception, on the steps after the 12:10: white elephant, ten dollars, nothing that eats. Thomas is going home to Idaho in a Tupperware to see snow. The Advent party: ran the white elephant like a cattle auction. Three steals and it’s frozen. Her Christmas card found me in the lobby on finals Monday — six true facts about hermit crabs; number six, they need a friend. She sent my family one too, praying for Nonna’s hand, and Ma stood it at the front of the mantel. Christmas Eve she wrote on my Wall. The first day back, on the steps of St. Brendan’s, she said she saw, and she’s happy for me. Over Christmas she prayed I’d be happy. Thomas saw snow. At the Haiti table: her grandmother prayed that rosary at the gate of the Sunshine Mine in 1972, eight days. On the eighth day two men came up. She lent Skye her apron. Skye wrote her a letter, on paper. It came on St. Agnes, with a surfboard drawn on the back.

body: The quarter is hers. The jukebox by the door takes it with the sound it makes for everybody, a swallow and a long mechanical think, and then Sam Cooke comes out of the speaker over the pie case, 1957, so easy he could be singing across a kitchen to somebody drying dishes. Skye walks back to the corner booth on the beat and slides in, and when Jack comes to the pass with a rack she mouths it at him through the window, every word, chin up, eyes shut on the long ones.

Outside, the storm has the wharf. It comes over the end of the pier in white sheets and runs back down the planks toward the street, and every time a big one lands the Anchor’s front windows shiver in their frames. Three harbor guys at the counter, waiting out the weather. A trucker with a newspaper. The door hasn’t opened since eight. Jack has been on since seven, and the dishes have been a trickle.

An hour ago Gloria set a slice of boysenberry in front of Skye, unasked, without slowing down, and Skye is eating it in small bites to make it last, with *Oceanography 1* propped open against the napkin dispenser at the chapter on fetch. Rudy is on the line in his hairnet, turning hash browns. The flat-top hisses. Rain runs down the window over the sink.

At nine Gloria goes into the office and comes back out with the Zenith off her desk held against her apron, the little one with the wood-grain sides and the channel dial, and sets it on the end of the counter by the register and runs the cord behind the pie case. “For storms and the World Series,” she says, to Jack, though he didn’t ask. She screws the cable from the wall by the register into the back of it and turns the dial to the channel out of Los Angeles, and stands back with her arms folded, and a lake comes up on the screen, a boarding school on a lake, in fall, every window lit.
“My granddaughter got me started,” Gloria says. “I watch for the clothes.”
In the corner booth Skye puts her fork down.

On the screen Cassidy comes down a staircase in a white wool peacoat with toggles, carrying a thermos. It’s night at Sweetwater Academy, and it’s raining there too, and her roommate is in the boathouse with a packed bag, meaning to row across the lake in the dark and never come back. Cassidy finds her. Cassidy pours her cocoa out of the thermos. Cassidy says the lake will still be there in the morning, and so will she, and takes off the peacoat and puts it around the roommate’s shoulders, and the music comes up under it like a bath running.
“That coat’s real wool,” Gloria says. “They spent money on that girl.” She watches Cassidy tuck the collar up around the other girl’s ears. “That one’s a vanilla custard. Nice. Nothing in it.”
“I’ve been telling them that for three seasons,” Skye says from the booth.
Gloria turns her head as far as the corner booth, and then back to the screen. “Then tell ’em louder, hon. Somebody needs to put some lemon in her.”
“What am I?” Skye says.
“You I did already,” Gloria says, and goes down the counter with the coffee.

“My mother’s watching this right now in Studio City with a legal pad.” Skye has pulled her knees up onto the bench. “She’ll call me at seven tomorrow with notes. I had a cold in this one. Listen.” On the screen Cassidy says *you’re safe, sweetie, you’re safe*, softly, to the girl in the coat. “You can hear it on the *s*. Three days of honey and the *s* still went.”

Her phone is face up on the table by the pie, as if seven o’clock might come early. He goes down the counter for the pot and fills her mug without being asked, and sets a second fork on the boysenberry plate so she has something to point at the screen with, and when he comes back from the pass she has stopped wincing at herself and started heckling.

Jack has never watched her on a screen with her in the room. He looks from the end of the counter to the corner booth and back: the girl in the white coat giving it away by a lake, all softness, every hair where somebody put it; and the girl in the booth with her knees up and his flannel on and purple on her bottom lip, mouthing her own lines a half-second ahead of herself and wincing at them. He likes the one in the booth so much it embarrasses him, at the pass, with a rack of cups in his hands.

At the flat-top Rudy has turned around with his spatula to scrape, and goes on scraping a grill that is already clean until the boathouse is over, with his eyes on the end of the counter. When Jack looks at him he goes back to his hash browns.

Before ten the harbor guys give up on the weather and go, and the Zenith is on the news with the sound down, and the Anchor is the trucker and the four of them and the storm. Skye comes up from the booth and sits on the last stool, by the pass, and puts an envelope on the steel shelf under the heat lamps and slides it through to him face up. One corner has gone soft from a week in her bag. On the front, in her block letters, it says TO DANNY COSTIGAN, and nothing else.
“I need the address,” she says. “I said that a week ago. I’ve been carrying him around.”

Jack takes the pen off the ticket wheel. Under her letters he writes DANIEL F. COSTIGAN, because the State of Ohio has never heard of a Danny, and after it the number, in his ordinary hand, small. He has known that number for two years. Under that he starts the second line: TRUMBULL CORRECTIONAL —

Rudy has come to the pass to set up the trucker’s plate. His eyes go down to the envelope on the steel as the second line goes onto it, and he turns back to the flat-top and picks up the spatula, and says it without turning around.
“Write the number big, *mijo*. They lose ’em if the number’s small.”
Gloria comes by for the trucker’s plate and reads the envelope upside down on her way past, like a ticket, and takes the plate.
Skye leans in over the steel to read the small number upside down.

The Sunday before Christmas, across a table in the visiting room at Trumbull, Danny asked him which one of them he could tell the truth to, and he didn’t have an answer for his brother. He has one now. His answer is leaning over the steel under the heat lamp in his flannel; she carried Danny around in her bag for a week to ask for that number. Nonna’s question, the one about which of them makes him pray, has the same answer. He hasn’t said either one to anybody. He doesn’t need to.

journal.title: Gloria (the Anchor)
journal.text: Hired me for rating her pie a four. Rated me a lattice-top. I’m not going to ask. Told her I won’t be the next guy at the door. She says nobody holds a door that long without somebody else walking through it. Asked after the pecan. I said she’s seeing somebody, he’s nice. She said lattice-top. Boxed a pie for Nonna. From a woman who’s been on her feet thirty years. Peach is August. St. Nicholas Eve, at the end of my shift, low, at the pass: ‘Pecan came to see if you were here.’ Gave my Thursday to Hector — his girl’s due at Christmas. ‘Don’t argue with a baby.’ Says I look like the pie case at closing. Rated somebody new. Boysenberry. ‘That one’s not waiting for any door.’ The last night: two forks and the pecan, at the counter. ‘That one’s still standing in it, hon.’ Thursday I asked her for Saturday night. ‘Who’s she?’ ‘You met her.’ ‘Boysenberry.’ She gave it to Rudy’s nephew. Her granddaughter got her watching *Sweetwater*; Thursdays at nine, for the clothes. She rated Cassidy a vanilla custard. Skye agreed.

Skye leans over the shelf on her elbows to watch it go down, and says it back to him under her breath when he’s finished, the letter and the numbers, so she has it too.

That if the number’s wrong or small it sits in a bin. And that mail call is the best part of any day inside, and an envelope from a girl in California, printed big, from somebody he’s never met, is going to be the best day of his month. Maybe of his year. Danny will read it on his bunk till it’s soft.

Skye takes the envelope back. She turns it over, and with her other hand cupped over the pen against the wet, she writes something on the flap, two lines, and he doesn’t see a word of it. She licks the flap again where it’s come unstuck and presses it down with her thumb and hands it back.
He goes over the number, big, his hand.

s18a.slug: THURSDAY · 11:00 PM · THE ANCHOR → THE FOOT OF THE WHARF → DELGADO HALL, THE CURB
body: The Zenith is the brightest thing left in the Anchor. Gloria has turned the sound up for the eleven o’clock news out of Los Angeles, and after the storm there is Conan O’Brien: NBC has made a deal to pay him something like thirty-two and a half million dollars to walk away, the newsman says, and money for his staff, and tomorrow night is his last show.
Jack says it to the cups he’s drying: “So somebody in Burbank meant something.”
“Correct,” Skye says, from the last stool. “For thirty-two and a half million dollars.”

The weather comes on, the Central Coast in green and yellow and a red blot sitting on top of Marisol, and Gloria takes the towel off Jack’s shoulder. “The wharf’s going under,” she says. “Go before you do.”

The blue mailbox at the foot of the wharf stands in an inch of running water. Skye keeps the envelope inside the slicker till the last possible second, then pulls the slot open and feeds Danny in and lets the lid bang shut on him, and pats the box twice on its wet head, like seeing somebody off at a train.
“What did you put in it?” he says, in the Saab, with the top up and the windows gone white. “Danny’s.”
“That’s between me and Daniel F.” She puts it in gear. “He can tell you if he wants. Brothers tell each other everything. I’ve seen movies.”

At the curb at Delgado the wipers go and the heater runs, and she leans across the gearshift and kisses him, slow, her wet hair cold against his cheek and her mouth warm and tasting of boysenberry, the slicker creaking every time she moves. Up and down the street the rain comes down on the parked cars.
“Tomorrow,” she says, against his mouth. “His last show. My house.”

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big.

s19.slug: THURSDAY · 11:34 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE 4TH-FLOOR HALL — KEVIN
body: Past eleven the fourth-floor hall runs on its night lights, one amber bulb in four, and the lounge, for once, is dark. The carpet is wet in two tracks from the stairwell door. Kevin is outside 420 in plaid pajama pants and the quarter-zip, with his BlackBerry held in both hands at belt height, looking down the hall at that door, and when it opens and it’s Jack, with the fryer from the Anchor in his clothes and the curb still on his mouth, he starts talking before it has finished moving.

“Hey. Jack. Hi. I was going to knock on 412, but Theo’s got the egg, and the egg’s a light sleeper, and I didn’t want to be the person who — so I waited out here, which I realize is strange, it’s been maybe ten minutes, Doug’s asleep, Doug sleeps like a — okay.” He takes a breath that doesn’t seem to get all the way in. “I rehearsed this. I want you to know I rehearsed this. Margot says that’s a mistake.”
“How long was the rehearsal?” Jack says.
“Four minutes. In the shower.”
“How did it go?”

“It went great. It was a different conversation.” He thumbs the dark trackball. “The Walk for Life is Saturday. San Francisco. The Newman van leaves at five a.m. — five, a.m., I know — and it gets back around midnight if nobody gets lost, and somebody always gets lost. Six hours each way. Clare’s going. Her brothers are probably going, all four, it’s a pro-life march in San Francisco, half the Bay Area is going, her brothers are a subset.” The pause that follows is the first one he’s taken. “I’d like you to come. For me.”

Kevin organizes. In five months Jack has watched him organize a beach cleanup, a carpool, and two flats of water for a Haiti table, and every time it was *we*: the group is going, somebody should, we’re all signing up. He has never heard Kevin ask for something with an I in it.
“Do you need a buffer?” Jack says. “For the brothers?”
“I need somebody who’ll lie about it afterward. She said she’d love for me to meet them, and I said great, and then I went and looked up the fastest way to Canada.”
“Is Lena going?” Jack says.
“It’s a Newman thing,” says Kevin, fast.

Kevin, who answers a yes-or-no question with a yes or a no and a related fact about the human body, has answered with a category. Jack knows what it means. Six hours each way is twelve in one van, with no door to leave by. And Saturday is the Anchor’s; he’ll have to go to Gloria for another one, and Osei’s *next Saturday* will have to wait a week.
He thinks about twelve hours of that. Then he looks at Kevin, in a hall at half past eleven with a four-minute rehearsal behind him and the BlackBerry gone dark in his hands, asking. That wins.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band. Wednesday he brought two flats of water to the Haiti table, which nobody asked for, and stayed to hold Clare’s violin case. ‘My mother knows your mother.’ Thursday he called Clare. His mother had the number, and his grandmother was on the speaker. She said yes to Sully’s. MLK Day he brought gloves for everybody. Tuesday in the basement he read us the first reading off his BlackBerry. Clare’s going to the Walk for Life, and so is he. He asked me to come — for him. I said yes.

choices.text: “Yes. For you.”
choices.key: Kevin asked you to the Walk for Life, for him. You said yes. For him.
response: The speed goes out of Kevin. For a moment he is only a pre-med in pajama pants in a hall. “Okay,” he says. “Okay. Thank you.”

Then the speed comes back in under a breath: “Bring a coat, bring a sandwich, don’t bring a sign unless you want to hold a sign for six hours — Clare says they’re heavier than they look — and gloves, I have gloves —” and he’s backing through the door of 420 with the BlackBerry held against his chest, and from inside the dark, Doug, asleep, says, “Dude.”

choices.text: “Five a.m. You owe me breakfast, Tran.”
choices.key: Kevin asked you to the Walk for Life. You said yes, and that he owes you breakfast.
response: “Done,” Kevin says. “Payable in gloves, net thirty.” He laughs, a short surprised one, and covers his eyes with the heel of the hand that has the BlackBerry in it. “I can’t believe I said it out loud. *I’d like you to come.* I sound like a wedding invitation.”
“You sound like a person.”
“I’ll work on it.” He points the BlackBerry at Jack. “You’re on the list.”
“What list?”
“There’s always a list.” And he eases the door of 420 open on a roommate who, from the sound of it, could not be woken by the Walk itself.

choices.text: “…Yeah. Okay.”
choices.key: Kevin asked you to the Walk for Life. You said yes.
response: “Thank you,” Kevin says. “Respectfully.”
It doesn’t follow, and he knows it doesn’t, and his ears go red in the amber light. “I don’t know why I said that.”
“It’s fine.”
“It’s five a.m.”
“I heard.”
“Oh-five-hundred,” Kevin says, as if that helps. He backs up to the door of 420 and finds the knob behind him on the second try.

body: The downspout outside 412 has been running since Tuesday, and tonight it has found a rhythm, a long pour and a knock, a long pour and a knock. Theo is sitting on the edge of his bed in the navy blazer with his phone in his hand, still damp at the shoulders, and the teacup on the nightstand beside him.
“That was Brooks,” he says. “Hollis has made it. Thursday to Thursday. I’m in.” He puts the phone face down on the blanket. “Brooks says I may keep him or eat him.”
“Congratulations, Brother Vance.”
“Please. It makes me sound like I make jam.”
“We should get him a plaque.”

“He’d hate it. He’s a very private egg.” Theo is smiling at the cup anyway. “I’m keeping him.” He picks up the cup in both hands and looks at the egg, the HOLLIS in somebody else’s blue ink, a week of stairwells and sandbags and storm and one salad bowl. He sets it back down on the nightstand exactly where it was.
“Hollis Ashby retires with honors.”
The cup sits on the nightstand in the lamplight, and the egg in it.
Theo looks around the room, at his own bed and the closet and the floor. “Costigan. My umbrella.”
“It lost an argument with the Supreme Court.”
“Most of us do,” Theo says, and turns out his lamp.
Jack moves his stapler to plug in the RAZR, and there’s a yellow Post-it under it, half-tucked, in Theo’s hand.

body.title: A Post-it, under the stapler
body.text: COMMUNICATION IS THE BEDROCK OF —

body: He holds it up to the desk lamp.
“That’s not for you,” Theo says, from the dark.
Jack puts it back under the stapler. He turns off the lamp and gets into bed, and the room goes to the streetlamp under the blind and the rain.
From the other bed:
“Over Christmas. You called her every night.”
Jack looks at the ceiling.
“Most nights.”
“Most nights,” Theo says, slowly, as if he’s writing it down.

He doesn’t say anything else, and Jack doesn’t ask him why he wants to know. It’s there in the room anyway, once it’s said: the garage on Glenwood Avenue with the door down, the cold coming up out of the concrete through his socks, the space heater’s orange coils, the phone hot against his ear, and her voice coming up the line from Louisiana, an hour at a time.
The RAZR buzzes on his chest.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’ MLK Day he shoveled sand one-handed for Sigma Rho with Hollis in the other. At midnight Wednesday he pitched me a movie about a man whose friend got dumped and was with somebody else in a week. He said it twice. Hollis made his week. Theo’s in. He’s keeping the egg.
